19775-vaughan-s-vegetable-cook-book-4th-:
Vaughan's Vegetable Cook Book, in its fourth edition, teaches cooking and using vegetables. Its guidance runs from soil to table. One passage covers forcing heads of leafy crops under manure-warmed soil. Fresh manure twelve inches thick, it advises, warms the bed slightly. That warmth hastens the making of the head. Vaughan's was a Chicago seed house serving home gardeners.

Cookbooks from seed firms doubled as garden manuals. Recipes sold seeds, and growing notes sold recipes. A fourth edition proves steady demand for both. The book preserves period varieties and period tastes together. Kitchen historians can trace how vegetables were raised and served. Few sources tie the garden bed to the dinner plate so directly.
19819-milton-s-comus:
John Milton wrote Comus, a masque, in 1634, when he was twenty-five. This edition, prepared by William Bell, adds an introduction and notes. Bell quotes Walter Bagehot's high estimate of the poem. Bagehot doubted any similar poem shows so well the mind's dignity. He found its sentiments tedious and its story uninteresting, yet praised it anyway. That tension shapes Bell's school edition.

Comus defends chastity and temperance in enchanted-wood scenes. A school edition must make its poetry teachable. Notes explain myth, language, and Milton's life. Bagehot's mixed verdict models honest criticism for students. The masque's music and moral argument still reward slow reading. Bell's volume shows Victorian schools keeping Milton central.
20181-a-defective-santa-claus:
A Defective Santa Claus, from 1904, is a Christmas tale told in lively dialect verse. Uncle Sid clucks, leans back laughing, and waves the sleigh away. He yells that the old horse ought to wear bells by now. Pa yells back that bells can wait till Santa comes this way.

Such verse tales ran in papers and gift books each December. Dialect spelling gives the jokes their rural, Hoosier-style flavor and bounce. Family, snow, and a flawed Santa drive the fun along. Readers get a short, warm dose of old Christmas humor in rhyme.
20732-the-carmina-of-caius-valerius-catu:
Catullus, a Roman poet of the first century before Christ, wrote short, fierce, and tender poems called the Carmina. The notes here grew in an odd way, drafted at a hotel table between courses. A Latin text sat open while talk went on around the writer.

Readers get love poems, insults, jokes, and grief in quick turns. Catullus can sound sweet in one line and brutal in the next. His voice feels startlingly modern across two thousand years. This edition pairs the poems with lively notes that show a reader working through the Latin line by line, with real delight.
20981-tristram-of-blent-an-episode-in-th:
A club man who once quit the Bar for letters fills Tristram of Blent's opening talk. He edits, not writes, by his own cheerful account of his trade. Anthony Hope sets this 1900 tale in an ancient house's long story.

Imposture, inheritance, and a fine old place drive Hope's polished plot. The true heir and a bold stand-in circle the Tristram name and lands. Hope, famed for The Prisoner of Zenda, writes with speed and sheen. This tale shows his lighter hand at work on English soil, with secrets in every portrait-hung room.
21858-the-daughters-of-danaus:
Marriage and a woman's right to her own growth are fought over in Mona Caird's The Daughters of Danaus, first published in 1894. The tale opens in a garret ballroom in an old keep, where dancers move to a reel in the moonlight. Celtic music sets nerves athrill even in the low-key scene. Caird's Scotland is wild, old, and full of pressure on its women.

An appendix prints Caird's own essay asking whether marriage hinders a woman's self-development. She had already scandalized Victorian readers by calling marriage a failure in print. The novel gives her argument flesh and landscape. It stands as one of the boldest feminist novels of the 1890s, still startling in its plain refusal of women's lot.
21909-a-military-genius:
Anna Ella Carroll of Maryland is called the great unrecognized member of Lincoln's Cabinet in this 1891 life by Sarah Ellen Blackwell. Blackwell compiled the book from family records and congressional documents. She had hoped Carroll herself would oversee the statements, but the family decided otherwise. The claim at the book's heart is bold: that Carroll, a woman, supplied key military thinking for the Union cause.

Carroll moved in Maryland politics and wrote pamphlets for the Union when her state wavered. Blackwell argues her plans reached Lincoln's war councils without public credit. The book was sold at the Woman's Journal office and suffrage rooms. It is at once a biography and a brief for women's uncounted public work, argued from papers her subject's family kept.
22004-the-genius:
Margaret Potter's novel The Genius came out in 1906, after her books Istar of Babylon and The House of De Mailly. The action opens on New Year's night in 1840, in the Russian town of Klin. Snow, church bells, and the old calendar set the scene. From there the tale follows a gifted young Russian as he grows up under the Czar's rule.

Chapters carry him through the Corps of Cadets, first love, and the Moscow Conservatoire. Music becomes the centre of his life, yet the secret police, the Third Section, watch men like him closely. Potter mixes court balls, camp life, and student folly with a darker strain of fate. The result is a big, earnest story of talent tested by power.
22270-bloom-of-cactus:
Robert Ames Bennet published Bloom of Cactus in 1919, a western novel of the Arizona desert. Its frontispiece shows Lennon raising his rifle to fire a parting shot over fleeing riders' heads. Lennon lingers on a ridge to enjoy the glorious view while his burro, uninterested in scenery, plods down the far trail. The desert light, not the animal, holds the man.

Bennet peoples the cactus country with prospectors, raiders, and a girl worth the title's bloom. Gunplay and desert craft move the plot in the pulp-western manner. Bennet wrote many such tales of the border country. This one keeps his formula: a hard land, a cool hero, and romance flowering where nothing should grow.
22521-the-young-acrobat-of-the-great-nor:
The Young Acrobat of the Great North American Circus promises big-top adventure. Its circus bills itself as an unparalleled show of many attractions. Never, the puff claims, has it embraced a greater variety.

World-famous acrobats headline the bill in large numbers. Clowns, bareback riders, and rope walkers fill out the ring. Trapeze artists and star performers complete the human cast. A colossal menagerie adds elephants, tigers, and lions. Leopards and other wild animals appear in great variety too. Behind that glitter stands the young acrobat of the title. His story takes readers inside circus life. Period boys read such books with sawdust in their dreams.
22875-circus:
A fall starts the trouble in Circus, a story told in the first person. The narrator broke no bones but was shaken up and left limping. The fall happened near the highway to the George Washington Bridge. From there he tried to flag down a ride, and his troubles found their road.

The circus of the title waits ahead of that roadside opening, with its own world of performers and risk. The telling stays plain and close, like a man recounting the strangest stretch of his life. Injury, travel, and the show business of big tops and small towns mix in the pages. Readers who like offbeat American storytelling will find a curious, grounded little narrative here.
22955-the-mistakes-of-jesus:
Bold questions drive The Mistakes of Jesus, a work of religious criticism dated 1932. Suppose a critic declares that Jesus lacked the highest intelligence. How, the book asks, can the critic be sure of his own judgment? How do you know your appraisal is right, lest you be found to fight against God? The author takes that challenge head-on rather than dodging it.

Page by page, the text examines sayings and actions of Jesus and judges them by reason and ethics. Believers of its day found the book shocking, and it was printed for a freethought readership that prized plain speaking. Its value now is historical as much as argumentative. It shows how far public criticism of scripture had come by the early twentieth century.
a-duet-with-an-occasional-chorus:
A. Conan Doyle's A Duet, with an Occasional Chorus appeared from Grant Richards in London in 1899, transcribed here from that edition. A letter to Maude Crosse frames the fiction as her private log, given by the author in January 1899. Two-oared boats putting out on the ocean stand for young married couples. The Overture is told in letters.

Frank Crosse and Maude Selby write their way from engagement at Woking and St. Albans to marriage. Chapters named like music — Two Solos, Keeping Up Appearances, The Trio — track the first years. Money trouble, a thundercloud, and danger test the duet. Doyle wrote the novel between Holmes stories, and his affection for ordinary happiness fills it. The chorus is the voice of friends and family around the pair. It remains his most personal fiction, a marriage manual disguised as a love story.
a-kidnapped-santa-claus:
L. Frank Baum wrote this Christmas story about the kidnapping of Santa Claus. It begins in the Laughing Valley, where Santa's castle stands and his helpers — ryls, knooks, pixies, and fairies — make toys all year. Next to the valley rise the caves of the Daemons: Selfishness, Envy, Hatred, and Malice, one in each cavern, with worse things rumored beyond.

The Daemons hate Santa precisely because he makes children happy, and they plot to stop his Christmas ride. Their capture of him leaves his helpers to deliver the toys in his place, scrambling through the night. Baum, the creator of Oz, gives the tale a moral machinery of temptations and repentance. It is a compact, darker companion to his better-known Christmas writings about Santa's life.
a-modern-telemachus:
Charlotte M. Yonge's A Modern Telemachus, reprinted here by Macmillan in 1889 from the 1886 first edition, takes its idea from Scott's Mariners' Chronicle. The Comte de Bourke was real: an Irish Jacobite naturalized in France, married to the Marquis de Varennes's daughter, and in high favor with Marshal Berwick. In 1719, with Spain and England at war, his family's voyage ends in wreck on a hostile shore. Yonge's preface insists that all that is most improbable in the tale is actual fact. The modern Telemachus is the young Arthur, thrust into adventures his tutor must survive beside him.

Inside, shipwreck, captivity among the Moors, and escapes test the boy as the Odyssey tested Telemachus, with a faithful mentor in the Mentor role. Yonge writes history's underside: Jacobite exiles, Spanish wars, and children carried through both. Readers get her historical fiction in compact form, a true story stranger than its romance dress.
a-village-stradivarius:
Kate Douglas Wiggin first printed her tale in The Village Watch Tower, and this 1904 Gay and Bird edition presents it on its own. It opens with a music lesson: a boy named Davy is told to find page three hundred and seventeen of the old instruction book and begin at the top. His teacher is the village music master, a man with one great treasure.

That treasure is a violin. He believes, or hopes, it to be a true Stradivarius. Around it gather the village, a love story, and a question of what the instrument is really worth. Wiggin writes rural New England with warmth and a light hand. The tale runs short and sweet, built on music and kindness.
albert-savarus:
Honoré de Balzac sets his novel in Besançon, in Ellen Marriage's translation, among the drawing rooms of the Restoration. The great house there belongs to the Baronne de Watteville, a proud heiress of the old Rupt family. Her young daughter watches the town's brilliant new lawyer, Albert Savarus, with growing fascination.

Savarus is able, ambitious, and silent about his past. The novel slowly uncovers the Italian love affair that shaped him and the vow that binds him still. Balzac builds the tale on letters, gossip, and political ambition in a provincial city. The ending, quiet and ironic, ranks among his most perfectly judged finishes.
alvira-the-heroine-of-vesuvius:
The Reverend A. J. O'Reilly presents his narrative as one culled from the traditions of a past generation, under the heading The Penitent Saints. His introduction admits the tale is sensational and defends printing records of sin and repentance against the false literature of the day. The scene opens in Paris a hundred and fifty years before his time.

Chapters move through a usurer, a mixed marriage, secret societies, flight, and tragedy in the mountains, with a funeral in the snow along the way. Alvira's story turns on sin, suffering, and repentance in the Catholic moral tradition. Vesuvius looms over the Italian parts of the tale. The book is old-fashioned melodrama with a preacher's purpose.
anti-federalist-papers-brutus:
The Brutus essays, sixteen in all, ran in New York papers across 1787 and 1788 against ratifying the Constitution. Brutus is thought to be Robert Yates, a New York judge and delegate who left the Philadelphia convention. The essays are the weightiest work of the Anti-Federalist side.

Brutus warns that a vast republic cannot stay free, and that the new federal courts and tax powers would crush the states. He predicts the Senate, the presidency, and the judiciary would drift into an aristocracy. The Bill of Rights owes much to pressure from Brutus and his allies. His losing side still frames American debates on federal power.
at-the-mercy-of-tiberius:
Augusta Evans Wilson's novel At the Mercy of Tiberius opens with a dying mother begging her daughter for one act of humility. Beryl refuses to beg her rich grandfather for help. Her pride, she answers, is for her mother, not herself. The mother dies with the reproach spoken. Beryl is left poor and alone, a grandfather's door shut against her. Evans Wilson, the Alabama author of St. Elmo and Beulah, builds her heroine's trials in the grand melodramatic manner.

General Darrington is then robbed and brutally murdered, and suspicion falls on Beryl. The district solicitor has no doubt of her guilt, and her trial becomes the town's sensation. Readers get the full Evans Wilson design: faith and pride tested by poverty, scandal, and a courtroom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-leub:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Leubus describes a celebrated ancient Cistercian abbey on the Oder, north-west of Breslau in Silesia. Its foundation deed of 1175 proved a forgery, but old Cistercian chronicles and Polish annals make Duke Boleslaus the Tall's foundation of August 1163 the most probable date.

Leubus' Cistercians did much for the cultivation and Germanisation of Silesia, then wilderness, forest, marsh and moor, though their work has been overrated. Daughter houses sprang from Leubus at Cracow, Münsterberg and Glatz, and the abbey held extensive possessions. Hussites burned it to the ground in 1432, and the Dukes of Sagan and Münsterberg later oppressed it for seven years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbo-cernuus: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Abbo Cernuus, meaning the crooked, describes a Paris Benedictine of St-Germain-des-Prés. He is sometimes called Abbo Parisiensis. Born around the mid-800s, Abbo was present at the Normans' siege of Paris in 885 to 886. He wrote a Latin verse account of it, with later events to 896, called De bellis Parisiacae urbis. He also left sermons for the instruction of clerics in Paris and Poitiers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-ortel:
Abraham Ortelius, also called Oertel, was an Antwerp-born cartographer, geographer, and archeologist, born 4 April 1527. He died there on 28 June 1598, his family having come from Augsburg, so he often styled himself Belgo-Germanus. After his father's death in 1535 left the family in difficulty, the young Ortelius traded in maps. He coloured charts and mounted them on canvas for resale, and at twenty he joined a guild to colour charts.

Map dealing carried him on long trips to Germany, England, and Italy and to the annual fair at Leipzig. Five years before Mercator's famous sea chart of 1569, Ortelius issued his great eight-sheet map of the world. Its only surviving copy sits at Basle. His chief work, the atlas that secures his place in cartography, gathers his own maps with those of others, and the entry draws on his letters and later scholarship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abundius:
Abundius was an Italian bishop born at Thessalonica early in the fifth century who died in 469 as Como's fourth bishop in Italy. He attended Constantinople's council in 450. At Chalcedon in 451 he fought the Eutychian heresy actively, as Pope Leo the Great's representative.

Milan's council of 452, convened to refute the same heresy, also saw him take part. The Te Deum's authorship is occasionally attributed to Abundius, among others. The entry cites Westcott and Tillemont, and its short compass makes it a compact record of a bishop known through councils rather than writings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abydus:
Abydus, or Abydos, was a Troas titular see in Asia Minor, under Cyzicus in the Hellespontic province. It stood at the Hellespont's narrowest point, where Asia and Europe nearly meet. Legend made the place famous as Leander's crossing to Sestus, to visit his mistress Hero.

Xerxes, too, built his famous bridge of boats in 480 BC, crossing with his troops to a headland on the far European shore. The entry cites Smith's dictionary of Greek and Roman geography, Mas Latrie's chronology, and Lequien's Oriens Christianus for readers tracing the ancient see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-accentus-eccl:
Accentus Ecclesiasticus is the counterpart of concentus in ancient church music. All liturgical song by the whole choir, or by a section of it, two or three singers, say, counted as concentus. Hymns, psalms, and alleluias generally fell under that term. By contrast, parts sung alone by priest, deacon, subdeacon, or acolyte counted as accentus.

Collects, Epistle and Gospel, and Preface fell in this class, in short anything kept chiefly to one tone, not sung, by priest or assistant. Harmonies, vocal or instrumental, must never accompany the accentus, though the concentus may receive accompaniment. The celebrant's Gloria in excelsis Deo and Credo in Unum Deum must not be repeated by the choir or backed by the organ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-accessus:
Accessus names conclave voting for a pope's election, by which a cardinal shifts his vote to another candidate. When votes have been counted after the first ballot and no candidate has the two-thirds majority, the next vote gives each cardinal a chance to change his vote. He does so by writing Accedo domino Cardinali and naming one of those already voted for, but not the cardinal he voted for before.

If he does not wish to change his vote, he may vote Nemini, for no one. Supplementary accession votes, added to a candidate's existing tally, must equal two-thirds of the total vote for an election. Otherwise ballots burn, and voting resumes the usual way the next day. The entry cites Lucius Lector on the conclave and Laurentius on ecclesiastical law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achaicus: Achaicus, a Corinthian Christian, joined Fortunatus and Stephanas in carrying the Corinthians' letter to St. Paul, and in bringing Paul's reply back to Corinth, as 1 Corinthians 16:17 records, with 16:15 alongside it. The entry gives this single errand and nothing more, a brief notice of a messenger trusted by both a church and its apostle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achiacharus:
The Vulgate's Tobias mentions Achiacharus only once, at 11:20, as Achior, but the Greek versions name him four times. There he appears as Tobias's nephew and an influential minister of Assyria's King Esarhaddon, who reigned 681 to 668 BC. That court position makes him a figure of weight in the Tobias story, despite his single Latin mention.

On the relation supposed by some critics between this personage and Ahiakar the Wise of eastern legend, the entry points readers to E. Cosquin in the Revue biblique Internationale of 1899. The short notice thus separates what scripture says from what legend may add, and leaves the identification as a critical question.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-actus-primus:
Actus primus, first actuality, is a technical expression in scholastic philosophy. Actus means determination, completion, or perfection, and in every being actualities stand in ordered series. Existence supposes essence, power supposes existence, and action supposes faculty. The first actuality begins a series, supposing no earlier actuality in that series, but calling for a further completion, the second actuality or actus secundus.

The same reality may count as actuality viewed from what precedes and as potency viewed from what follows, so first actuality shifts with the point where the series begins. Primary matter is pure potency, and substantial form is its first form. Quantity is a first actuality beside shape, and power beside action, which is the most frequent use: the faculty is first actuality, its exercise second. Seeing in actu primo means having sight, while seeing in actu secundo means actually seeing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-actus-purus:
Actus purus, pure act, is a scholastic term for God's absolute perfection. All finite beings hold actuality with potentiality, perfection with imperfection. Primary matter, the basis of material substance, is pure potentiality. Change supposes a potential element, since it moves from potency to act, and material things change in substance, quantity, quality, place, and activity.

Angels, as pure spirits, escape changes tied to matter, yet they still hold imperfection and potentiality. Their existence depends on another, their actions come one after another and stand apart from their faculty of acting. Since all things hold some potency, there must exist a being from whom potency is wholly excluded, who is simply actuality and perfection, Actus Purus. Actuality, the entry argues, must precede potency, since change presupposes a being already in act.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-scotus:
Adam Scotus, or the Premonstratensian, was a late-twelfth-century theologian and church historian. Born either in Scotland or England, he joined St. Norbert's newly founded order. He is also believed to have become Whithorn's Abbot and Bishop — Candida Casa in Scotland — dying after 1180.

His works include Sermones, a Liber on the order, habit, and profession of Premonstratensian canons, sometimes called a commentary on St. Augustine's Rule, De Tripartito Tabernaculo, De Triplici Genere Contemplationis, and two books of Soliloquies on the instruction of the soul. He ranked among the Middle Ages' most appreciated mystical authors, his works showing unusual sweetness and spirituality in style and matter. He also goes by Adam Anglicus and Anglo-Scotus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adeodatus:
Adeodatus, son of St. Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, was born in 372 and died in 388. Augustine was not converted until thirty-two. At seventeen he had formed an illicit relation with a young woman, whose child Adeodatus was. Augustine, delighted, named him Adeodatus, meaning gift of God; Augustine's move to Rome and later Milan took woman and child with him.

The boy was his parents' pride and hope, possessed of an extraordinary mind. Monica, Augustine's mother, wished him to marry the child's mother, hoping grace would then enlighten his mind. Finally the pair separated, and the woman, stronger than Augustine, returned to Carthage and entered a monastery. Adeodatus appears as interlocutor in his father's De beata vita and contributed largely to De Magistro two years later. He seems to have died soon after, aged sixteen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adrian-turneb:
Adrian Turnebus was a philologist born at Andely in Normandy in 1512, who died at Paris on 12 June 1565. Accounts of his life are scanty and partly contradictory. His name is said to come from a Scottish gentleman named Turnbull, settled in Normandy, whose name took the French form Tourneboeuf, then Tournebu and Turnebe, in Latin Turnebus. He came from a noble though poor family.

Sent to Paris at eleven, his ability soon surpassed pupils and teachers alike. He took his Master of Arts in 1532, taught humanities at Toulouse for fourteen years, then became professor of Greek at Paris, exchanging that chair for Greek philosophy in 1561. With William Morel he supervised the royal Greek press from 1552 to 1555. Over-study wore him out early, and he died at fifty-three, buried without religious ceremony by his own direction, raising the question whether he stayed Catholic or leaned Protestant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aeris-of-pont:
Aeris of Pontus, friend and fellow ascetic of Eustathius, saw him become Sebaste's bishop in 355 and ordained Aerius, placing him over that city's hospital or asylum. Aerius fell out with Eustathius, upbraided him for deserting ascetic practices, and began preaching new doctrines. He insisted no sacred character set bishop or priest apart from laymen.

He also held that keeping Easter was a Jewish superstition, that prescribing fasts or abstinences by law was wrong, and that praying for the dead was useless. Some say jealousy of Eustathius inspired these doctrines. For a time Sebaste gave him many followers, but his tenets never caught on, and he and his sect gradually became an occasion of abuses that made them odious. Protestants count his movement important as an early hint of their views, while his contemporaries firmly opposed him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aetius:
Aetius was a Roman general, patrician, and consul, born toward the end of the fourth century, who died in 454. Son of an Italian mother and the Scythian soldier Gaudentius, he spent his youth as hostage to Alaric, learning war from him, and to Rugila, king of the Huns. That experience gave him the prestige that formed both his power's basis and his fall's source.

This man who delivered Europe from the Huns first appears leading 60,000 Huns for the usurper Johannes in 424. After Johannes's execution, Aetius was pardoned and restored to Empress Placidia's favour. Made count, probably of Italy, he became chief adviser to Placidia and Valentinian III. Conflict with Bonifacius, Count of Africa, followed. Boniface fell near Rimini, Aetius retired to the Huns, returned to power at Ravenna in 433, and ruled seventeen more years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agabus:
Agabus, a New Testament prophet, appears in Acts 11:28 and 21:10. Most probably both passages name the same person, who appears to have lived at Jerusalem; tradition counts him among the seventy-two disciples of Luke 10:1 and one of Antioch's martyrs. The Roman Martyrology names him on 13 February; Greek commemoration falls on 8 March.

Acts 11:27-30 has Agabus predicting the famine identified with the one in Claudius's fourth year, AD 45; in 58 the prophet predicted St. Paul's coming captivity, though he could not persuade the apostle to stay away from Jerusalem, as Acts 21:10-11 records. The short entry thus ties one prophet to two predictions, famine and imprisonment, across thirteen years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agapetus:
Agapetus, deacon of Constantinople's Sancta Sophia church around 500 and reputed tutor of Justinian, authored exhortations in 72 short chapters addressed about 527 to that emperor. Each chapter's first letters form a dedicatory acrostic reading: The very humble Deacon Agapetus to the sacred and venerable Emperor Justinian. The little work treats a ruler's moral, religious, and political duties in general terms.

In form it is sententious and rhetorical throughout, closely resembling a similar work in the Barlaam and Joasaph romance. Both seem drawn from Isocrates and from Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus. Medieval teachers found the work eminently suited, by its edifying content, pure Greek diction, and skilful construction. Latin, French, and German translations followed, highly commended by Renaissance humanists, and saw some twenty editions in the sixteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agathangelus:
Agathangelus, supposed secretary to Armenia's King Tiridates II, lends his name to a life of Gregory the Illuminator, Armenia's first apostle, dead about 332. It purports to exhibit Gregory's deeds and discourses, and survives in Armenian and in Greek. Greek scholars now recognize the Greek text as a translation, probably made late in the sixth century, while the Armenian original dates to the latter half of the fifth.

Von Gutschmid maintains the unknown author used a genuine life of St. Gregory, a history of his martyrdom, and one of St. Ripsime and her companions. Fact and legend mingle in this life with legendary additions, woven into unity by the narrator. He may have taken his name from his quality as teller of Armenia's conversion good news, Agathaggelos. The Armenian text was printed at Constantinople and Venice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agrippinus:
Agrippinus was Carthage's bishop at the second century's close and the third's beginning. During his episcopacy the African Church faced a question about converts from schism or heresy. Those previously Catholic fell under church discipline and penance. But for those baptized outside the Church, was their baptism valid? Agrippinus called Numidia and Africa's bishops to Africa's First Council, probably 215-217, which answered negatively.

He therefore decided on absolute, not conditional, baptism for such persons. Heretics, it was argued, lack true faith and cannot absolve from sin, so their baptismal water cannot wash sin away. These reasons seemed to warrant his conclusion, though it was not Roman usage, and the point had not yet been definitely settled. Half a century later Cyprian praised his continuous good repute, and Augustine defended him against the Donatists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-pighiu:
Albert Pighius was a Dutch theologian, mathematician, and astronomer, born at Kampen about 1490 and dead at Utrecht in December 1542. At Louvain he studied philosophy and started theology; Adrian of Utrecht, the future Pope Adrian VI, taught him there. He completed his studies at Cologne and took his doctorate in theology in 1517. He followed Adrian to Spain and then to Rome, where he served under Clement VII and Paul III.

His mathematical and astronomical writings include a defence of astrology against vulgar fortune-tellers. They also include a treatise on reforming the calendar addressed to Leo X and replies to Marco Beneventano on astronomy. As a theologian he defended the Church's authority against the Reformers, above all in his Assertion of the Church Hierarchy of 1538, a reply to Henry VIII. The entry notes, however, that some of his teachings on original sin and justification strayed from the Catholic position.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albinus:
Albinus was a scholarly English monk, a pupil of Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Adrian of St. Peter's, Canterbury, and a contemporary of St. Bede. He succeeded Adrian as abbot and was laid beside him in 732. His chief claim to fame is that Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English owes its making to him. Bede says the work was chiefly owing to Albinus's prompting and help.

Bede calls Albinus supremely learned across the sciences. and records his debt in the letters that preface the History. One letter was sent to Albinus himself and one to King Ceolwulf. Albinus supplied what had happened in Kent since St. Augustine's arrival, in church and civil matters alike, and helped fit Roman documents brought back by Nothelm into their proper places. The entry credits him with a fine historical sense and earnest diligence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alcimus:
Alcimus, whose name probably renders the Hebrew Eliakim, was high priest and leader of the Hellenizing party in Judaea in the time of Judas Maccabeus. Though not of high-priestly stock, he won favour at court by opposing the religious and national feelings of his countrymen. Lysias, regent for Antiochus Eupator, appointed him high priest in 162 B.C. Opposition from the Maccabean party kept him from exercising the office.

Alcimus turned to Demetrius Soter, who had overthrown Eupator, denounced Judas and his followers as rebels, and was reappointed with Bacchides sent to install him by force. The slaughter of sixty leading Assideans and the cruelties of Bacchides only strengthened the Maccabees, and after Judas died fighting Bacchides at Elasa in 160 B.C., Alcimus pressed his Hellenizing policy and persecuted the faithful to the law. He was struck with paralysis that same year and died in great suffering.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aldus-manutiu:
Aldus Manutius, or Aldo Manuzio, was a scholar and printer born at Sermoneta near Rome in 1450 and dead in 1515. He read Latin at Rome and Greek at Ferrara, and in 1482 went to Mirandola, where Pico made him tutor to his nephews, Alberto and Lionello Pio, Princes of Carpi. At Carpi in 1490 he conceived his bold plan of a Greek press at Venice, funded by his former pupil Alberto Pio.

Between 1494 and 1515 the Aldine press issued thirty-three first editions of the greatest Greek authors, including Aristotle's works from 1495 to 1498. Aldus's house became a gathering place for Greek scholars. His aim was the finest books at the smallest prices. His Greek, Latin, and Italian library, begun in 1501, used the italic type known as Aldine. In 1499 he married the daughter of the Venetian printer Andrea Torresano, joining their two houses, and his son Paulus succeeded him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-heg:
Alexander Hegius was a Dutch humanist, born probably in 1433 at Heeck in Westphalia and dead at Deventer in December 1498. Nothing is known of his early studies, but he was already mature when ordained a priest. He called himself a pupil of Rudolph Agricola, the leading voice of earlier German humanism, who, though eleven years his junior, greatly influenced him.

In 1474 Hegius took charge of the school at Deventer, already famous. There he taught pure Ciceronian Latin and Greek and remade the course around the classics, sweeping away the old schoolbooks. More than two thousand students often gathered there, and he inspired them with zeal for study and for teaching itself. Among his pupils were Erasmus, Murmellius, and Mutianus, and shortly before his death he gave all he had to the poor of Deventer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-sev:
Alexander Severus was a Roman emperor, born at Acco in Palestine in 208 and murdered by his mutinous soldiers on the Rhine in 235. His parents were Genessius Marcianus and Julia Mamaea, and was called Alexianus in youth. When his cousin Elagabalus was murdered in 222, Alexander took the throne. His mother directed his education at Antioch, where she invited the Christian teacher Origen between 218 and 228.

The entry records many signs of Alexander's goodwill toward the new religion. He set images of Abraham and Christ in his private chapel, allowed the free exercise of the Christian faith, and had Christ's golden rule engraved on the palace walls. He even considered building a temple to Christ, but held back when told the other gods would soon cease to be honoured. Yet Christians still suffered under his mild reign, and some writers place St. Cecilia's death for the faith in his time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloisius-lili:
Aloisius Lilius, chief author of the Gregorian Calendar, came from Cirò in Calabria. His name was originally Aloigi Giglio. Montucla wrongly calls him Veronese, and Delambre confuses him with Lilius Gregorius Giraldi. Little is known of his life beyond his Perugia medicine professorship. The claim of a Roman physician dying in 1576 is apparently unsupported. In 1576 his brother Antonius presented his calendar-reform manuscript to the Roman Curia.

Lilius's work needs the earlier efforts and the shape of his reform to be understood. General councils carried the reform from the start, from Nicaea in 325 through Constance, Basle, the Fifth Lateran, and Trent. The entry traces the councils, the Avignon conference in 1344, and the fifteenth-century work of Pierre d'Ailly and Nicolas de Cusa. It follows the commission weighing his manuscript, whose contents survive only in its report and Ciaconus's Compendium, printed by Clavius. The bull Inter Gravissimas promulgated the reform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloysius-bell:
Aloysius Bellecius was a Jesuit ascetic author, born at Freiburg im Breisgau in 1704 and died at Augsburg in 1757. He taught philosophy one year, theology seven, and spent four years among South America's Amazon Indians. Recalled to Europe, he cared for his brethren spiritually and later directed the Porrentruy seminary in the Diocese of Basle. He wrote a number of Latin ascetical works, most translated and often reprinted.

Most noteworthy: Christian Dying Piously (1749), Chief Hindrances, Aids, and Incentives of Solid Virtue (1755), Marrow of Asceticism, or Exercises of St. Ignatius (1757), and Sacred Triduum (1757). English translations of the last three remain in print. Solid Virtue was translated from the French in London in 1887. Spiritual Exercises according to St. Ignatius was translated from Bresciani's Italian version by William Hutch in 1876, with some opinions softened as too rigid. Solid Virtue: A Triduum and Spiritual Conferences was translated by John Holtzer, published in New York in 1882.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alumnus:
Alumnus, from Latin alo, to nurse or feed, means in church usage a student preparing for ministry in a seminary. Originally it meant an adopted child with restricted privileges, or foster child, but since Trent it equals seminarian, often in Rome's colleges. Trent required bishops to found priesthood schools; candidates had been taught in priests' houses, monasteries, or universities.

Trent's alumni were at least twelve, able to read and write, of hopeful disposition, poor children especially favoured. They studied philosophy, theology, scripture, canon law, rites, sacred eloquence, and plain chant. Bishops were to see them hear Mass daily, confess monthly, communicate as advisable, join cathedral festivals, and visit often, watching learning and piety. In 1896 the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars ruled alumni at universities must not associate too familiarly with other students.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alvarus-pelag:
Alvarus Pelagius, or Alvaro Pelayo, celebrated writer born in Spain about 1280, died at Seville in 1352. He studied canon law at Bologna, resigned his benefices in 1304, and entered the Franciscans, reportedly Duns Scotus's pupil and tutor to Don Pedro of Portugal's children. He became penitentiary to John XXII at Avignon, enjoyed the pope's favour, and refuted antipope Pietro Rainalducci's claims.

He later became titular Bishop of Coron and then Bishop of Sylves in Portugal. He served as Apostolic nuncio there, and was buried at Seville's Monastery of St. Clare, never cardinal despite some claims. His De planctu ecclesiae, begun at Avignon in 1330, completed in 1332, defends church rights and rebukes church abuses with freedom and force. First published at Ulm in 1474, with Venice and Lyons editions following, it drew debate over his poverty views, which Sbaralea defends.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amathus:
The name Amathus covers two ancient titular sees: one in Syria, suffragan of Apameia, its episcopal list known from 449 to 536. The other stands on Cyprus's southern coast, its list running from the fourth century to 787. The Cypriot city was among the island's most ancient Phoenician settlements, long keeping an Oriental town's customs, character, and worship.

It was famed for Aphrodite and Adonis worship and of the Tyrian god Melkart. Its great wheat fields and rich mines were celebrated in antiquity, Ovid naming them in book ten of the Metamorphoses, verse 220.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrose-pelar:
Ambrose Pelargus, born Stork at Nidda in Hesse about 1488, died at Trier in 1557. The Dominican, famed for eloquence and elegant writings, knew Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. He aimed his polemics chiefly at Anabaptists, Iconoclasts, and Mass rejecters. He attended Worms's Diet in 1540 and Trent in 1546 as the Archbishop of Trier's theologian and procurator, addressing the Fathers on 10 May 1546.

When the Council moved to Bologna in 1547, Charles V, angered by his favouring the transfer, had the archbishop recall him, yet chose him again as theologian in 1561. His chief works defend the Eucharistic sacrifice against Oecolampadius, oppose Anabaptists and Iconoclasts, and render Chrysostom's liturgy from Greek into Latin, with letters exchanged with Erasmus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amisus: Amisus is a Pontic titular see in Asia Minor, a wealthy trading centre under Pontus's kings. It was a royal residence and fortress of Mithridates, its territory including the fabled Amazons' dwelling place. Trade, kingship, and legend thus meet in one Pontic see, rich in commerce, fortified by kings, and storied at once.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anastasius-bi:
Librarian of the Roman Church, Anastasius was born about 810 and died in 879. A nephew of Bishop Arsenius of Orta, he learned Greek from Greek monks and won an education unusual for his age. He ranks here as the most learned churchman of Rome in the rough ninth century.

Under Pope Nicholas I he served as abbot of a monastery in Trastevere and translated Greek works into Latin, including a life of Saint John the Almsgiver. Adrian II then made him librarian, an office that brought great influence at the papal court. Sent as envoy to Constantinople in 869, he attended the last session of the Eighth Council in 870 and defended the papal cause with effect. He also shared in revising the life of Nicholas I.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anazarbus: Anazarbus was a titular metropolitan see of Cilicia, in Lesser Armenia, suffragan to Antioch. The ancients also knew it as Nova Troas, the crusaders as Naversa, and the Arabs as Ain-Zarba. Councils met there in 431 and 435, and the short article gives little beyond its names, its rank, and those councils.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andreas-vesal:
Andreas Vesalius, the reorganizer of anatomy, was born at Brussels in 1514 and died on his journey home from Jerusalem in 1564. Son of Andreas Vesalius, court-apothecary to Charles V, he came from a German family of physicians from Wesel. As a boy he dissected animals with great interest.

After early studies at Louvain, he went to Paris about 1533 and publicly dissected a corpse at his teachers' request. In 1536 he made at Louvain the first public dissection in eighteen years. In 1537 he went to Padua, took his medical degree, and became professor of anatomy, dissecting bodies himself. In 1538 he published the Tabulae anatomicae. In 1540 he began his celebrated Fabrica, completed in 1543. His work showed Galen had never dissected a human body, destroying belief in his authority. In 1544 he became court physician to Charles V, later serving Philip II. In 1564 he undertook the Holy Land pilgrimage from which he never returned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelus:
The Angelus is a short devotion honouring the Incarnation, repeated morning, noon, and evening at the bell. It consists in three Hail Marys, with introductory versicles and a concluding prayer added later. The prayer belongs to Our Lady's antiphon, Alma Redemptoris, and is not strictly required for the indulgence. From the first versicle, Angelus Domini nuntiavit Mariae, the devotion takes its name.

Benedict XIII granted 100 days per recitation, with a monthly plenary, in 1724, modified by Leo XIII in 1884. Originally it was said kneeling, except on Sundays and Saturday evenings. In origin it imitated monastic custom. A Franciscan decree of Bonaventure's time had the laity say Hail Marys at the Complin bell, since at this hour Our Lady was saluted by the angel. The fuller form cannot be traced earlier than 1612. In Italy a De profundis for the holy souls followed the evening Angelus, with three Glorias for the Trinity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthemius:
High rank and fine character marked Anthemius, a Byzantine official of the fourth and fifth centuries. He counted among the most celebrated magistrates of his day, known for wisdom and administrative ability. Saint Chrysostom and he held each other in the greatest respect. When disturbances followed Saint Chrysostom's deposition at Easter 404, Anthemius, as Magister Officiorum, faced demands from the saint's enemies for troops to disperse the crowd.

At first he refused, then gave in to their pressure, declaring that they bore responsibility for the consequences. He became consul in 405, and soon after Prefect of the East, an office he held until 417. Saint Chrysostom wrote to him in warm terms. A law of 28 April 406 gives him the title of Patrician. He advised Theodosius the Younger as principal adviser, and through his daughter's marriage to Procopius he became grandfather to the Emperor Anthemius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anton-brus:
Anton Brus, archbishop of Prague, was born in Moravia in 1518 and took charge of a see empty for 140 years. A member of the Knights of the Cross, he served as army chaplain in the Turkish war and became grand master of his order at thirty-four. In 1558 he became bishop of Vienna, and in 1561 archbishop of Prague.

Ferdinand sent him to Trent as Bohemia's legate to the council, where he urged that Utraquists, who took communion in both kinds, be allowed the practice in hopes of reunion. Back in Prague he fought to restore Catholic life against Hussite strength and weak imperial backing. After his death in 1580, Bohemian Catholics kept losing ground until the White Mountain victory of 1620.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoninus-piu:
Antoninus Pius, Roman emperor from 138 to 161, was born in 86 at Lanuvium near Rome. After a consulship in 120 and service as proconsul in Asia, Hadrian adopted him as successor on condition he adopt Marcus Aurelius in turn. He shared power with Hadrian until the old emperor's death, then ruled alone in what historians call Rome's most peaceful and prosperous reign.

A Stoic in private life, he kept a simple court, guarded frontiers without wars of conquest, and put down revolts swiftly. Toward Christians he kept Trajan's procedure, and his tolerant temper let bishops meet in councils on a new scale. The entry credits his reign with order, mercy, and the growth of Christian unity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonius: Antonius is the name behind a Latin Christian poem of the third century, Antonii carmen adversus gentes, printed in Migne's Latin fathers. Gallandi linked it to an otherwise unknown Antonius, imagined as living in Commodian's day. Muratori, as Bardenhewer reports, showed the poem belongs instead to Paulinus of Nola, who lived from 351 to 431. Two editions, by Oehler in 1847 and Bursian in 1880, likewise assign it to Paulinus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonius-augu:
Historian of canon law Antonius Augustinus, born at Saragossa in 1517 and dead at Tarragona in 1586, became archbishop of Tarragona after a career in law, diplomacy, and church reform. After study at Alcalá and Salamanca he travelled to Bologna, Padua, and Florence. There he examined the famous Florentine codex of the Pandects, the Roman law digest, and met scholars of the new historical school. He took his doctorate in civil and canon law in 1541 and became auditor of the Rota in 1544.

Sent to England in 1555 with congratulations for Queen Mary, he later became bishop of Alife and then of Lérida. He spent three years at the Council of Trent urging reform of the clergy. He blamed church faults for unrest in France and Germany and pressed for change from within. The entry presents a scholar-bishop who treated old church law with critical care rather than blind reverence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonius-poss:
Mantua-born Jesuit Antonius Possevinus, who lived from 1533 or 1534 to 1611, served as theologian and papal envoy across northern Europe. At sixteen he went to Rome to learn, learned many languages, and became secretary for Cardinal Ercole Gonzaga. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1559, preached against heresy in Savoy, was ordained in 1561, and preached in Paris, Bayonne, Rouen, and elsewhere, winning over many Calvinists. He later led colleges at Avignon and Lyons and became secretary to the Jesuit general in 1573.

When King John III of Sweden wished to become Catholic, Pope Gregory XIII sent Possevinus as special legate in 1577, dressed as a layman. The king made his profession of faith. Talks on converting Sweden ran into many difficulties, and Possevinus returned to Rome with proposals. The entry follows a linguist-diplomat whose missions linked Rome to Sweden, Bavaria, and Bohemia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apocrisiarius:
An apocrisiarius, from a Greek word for answer, was an ecclesiastical envoy of Christian antiquity, sent to high church or royal courts. In the East, patriarchs kept their envoys at the imperial court, and metropolitans, or archbishops, kept theirs at patriarchal courts. Popes likewise sent clerics of the Roman church to settle important questions, fix points of discipline in local dioceses, or guard church interests in religious disputes. The letters of Gregory the Great, pope from 590 to 604, mention such envoys, called responsales, very often.

Relations between popes and the imperial court at Constantinople grew most important after the fall of the Western Empire in 476 and during great doctrinal disputes in the Greek church. Papal representatives there gradually became permanent legates and ranked as the most important and responsible of papal envoys. The entry explains an office that joined diplomacy to church government in the ancient world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apollonius-of:
Apollonius of Ephesus, an anti-Montanist Greek church writer active between 180 and 210, likely from Asia Minor, defended the church against Montanus and his movement. Montanism, a movement from Phrygia, claimed fresh revelations through Montanus and his prophetesses. Apollonius followed earlier opponents such as Zoticus of Comanus and Apollinaris of Hierapolis. A later work, Praedestinatus, calls him bishop of Ephesus, yet the silence of other writers makes that claim doubtful.

His own work is lost, not even its title surviving, yet Eusebius cites it and Jerome praises it. From those citations the article rebuilds its case. It exposed Montanist prophecies as false. It told unedifying stories of Montanus and his prophetesses and spread the report of their suicide by hanging. It named followers such as Themison, who dodged martyrdom with money, and the false martyr Alexander. Readers meet early orthodoxy arguing through biography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arabissus: Arabissus was a titular see, a former bishop's seat now given as a title, in Armenia, under Melitene. Its bishops' list is known from 381 to 692, as given by Gams. Le Quien's Oriens Christianus supplies the source for the see. The entry records little more than its place in the Armenian church's hierarchy and the span of its known bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archiereus: Archiereus, in Russian arkhierei, is a Greek word for bishop viewed as the culmination, or highest point, of the priesthood. It is much used in Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic service books for services matching the pontifical services of the Roman rite. Those services are led by a bishop in full vesture. The word must not be confused with protoiereus, or archpriest, the highest rank a married priest may reach in the Greek church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ardo-smaragdu:
Ardo Smaragdus, a hagiographer, or writer of saints' lives, died at the Benedictine monastery of Aniane in southern France in March 843. He entered that monastery as a boy and grew up under Abbot Benedict of Aniane. For piety and talent he was ordained and placed at the head of the monastery school. In 794 he went with his abbot to the Council of Frankfurt, and in 814 he became abbot in Benedict's place. Benedict had moved to the imperial court at Aix-la-Chapelle at Louis the Pious's invitation.

Honoured as a saint in his own monastery, Smaragdus wrote a life of Benedict of Aniane for the monks of Cornelimünster, where Benedict had died. Written in 822, it counts among the most reliable saints' lives of its period. Mabillon edited it in his Acts of the Benedictine Order, from which it was reprinted in Migne's Latin fathers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ariassus: Ariassus was a titular see, a former bishop's seat now given as a title, in Pamphylia in Asia Minor. Its bishops' list from 381 to 458 is given in Gams. Le Quien's Oriens Christianus and Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography are cited as sources. The entry records the see's place and the span of its known bishops, nothing more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arius:
Arius, a heresiarch, or founder of heresy, was born about AD 250, said to be Libyan by descent, son of Ammonius, and died in 336. Having learned his views from Lucian, presbyter of Antioch and later martyr, he sided in 306 with Meletius, an Egyptian dissenter, against Peter, bishop of Alexandria. Reconciliation followed, and Peter ordained Arius deacon, but further disputes led the bishop to expel his restless churchman.

Arius then won the friendship of Achillas, Peter's successor, who made him presbyter in 313 and gave him charge of Baucalis, an Alexandria district, where he could expound Scripture officially. In 318 his quarrel with Bishop Alexander erupted over Christ's divine sonship and substance, the heart of Arianism. Condemned at Alexandria in 321 by a synod of nearly a hundred Egyptian and Libyan bishops, he drew many Syrian prelates to his side.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnaldus-vill:
Arnaldus Villanovanus, or Arnald of Villanova, Villeneuve, or Bachuone, was celebrated in his day as physician, pharmacist, and alchemist. He was born between 1235 and 1240 and dead at sea near Genoa in 1312 or 1313. Most details of his life are obscure, including his home town, whose Latin form Villanova fits towns in Spain, France, and Italy. Some place it at Villanueva in Catalonia, others at Villeneuve-Loubet in France. He died while sailing to visit the sick pope, Clement V.

Well versed in classical languages, Hebrew, and Arabic, he knew all then known of natural science, above all medicine and pharmacology, the study of drugs. At Barcelona he studied under John Casamila, prized Galen, and among Arabs cared only for Rhazes. He taught botany, medicine, and alchemy at Barcelona, Montpellier, and Paris, living a wandering life among those cities and courts. The entry presents a healer whose learning crossed languages and borders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnobius:
Arnobius, a Christian apologist who flourished under Diocletian, emperor from 284 to 305, had first been a distinguished rhetorician at Sicca in Roman Africa. Jerome says he owed his Christian faith to a dream. To convince the local bishop of his earnest belief, he wrote about 305 a seven-book apologetic work. Jerome calls it Adversus Gentes; it is Adversus Nationes in the sole ninth-century manuscript that survives.

He vigorously defends Christian monotheism, belief in one God, described as chief and highest God, and the divinity of Christ and of Christianity. That divinity is proved by its rapid spread, its sway over uncivilized peoples, and its accord with the best philosophers. On Plato's Christian leanings he left a remarkable treatise on the soul's nature, and he refutes pagan idolatry at length. The entry presents a convert rhetorician turned defender of the faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asmodeus:
Asmodeus is the demon named in the Book of Tobit, chapter three. His name most probably comes from a Hebrew root meaning to destroy, matching Abaddon, the Destroyer, in Revelation 9:11. Tobit tells that the virgin Sarah, kinswoman of Tobias, had been given in turn to seven husbands, all slain on their wedding nights before marriage was consummated.

Superstition grew that the demon loved the maiden and killed her husbands from jealousy, and the Greek Tobit says young Tobias himself was moved by that superstition. The inspired text nowhere approves it: God allowed the demon to kill those men because they entered marriage with unholy intentions. The pious Tobias, guided by Raphael, marries Sarah, Raphael expels the demon, and Tobias's chastity and temperance stand as the tale's moral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aspendus: Aspendus was a titular see in Pamphylia in Asia Minor, set along the Eurymedon river on a lofty hill commanding a view of the distant sea. Its bishops' list from 325 to 787 is given in Gams. Le Quien's Oriens Christianus and Smith's Dictionary of Christian Geography are cited, and the entry records the see's riverside hilltop site and the span of its known bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assuerus:
Assuerus is the name of two different biblical persons. First, in Ezra 4:6 and Esther, it matches Hebrew Achashwerosh and denotes Xerxes I, king of Persia. Samaritans addressed complaints against Jerusalem's inhabitants to him soon after 485 BC, early in his reign. The king, intent on pleasures and war with Egypt, seems to have disregarded the charges.

Herodotus reports that Xerxes called a council of nobles in his third regnal year to debate war against Greece. That matches Esther's account of a great feast for nobles in that same year. In his seventh year, after returning from the Greek war, Esther became queen, and in his twelfth year Esther saved Jews from the ruin planned by Haman. A second Assuerus appears elsewhere in scripture, and the entry separates the Persian king from his namesake.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asterius:
Asterius is the name of several notable persons in early Christian history, and the article sorts them. Asterius of Petra, a bishop of Arabia, was ill-treated by the Arian faction at Sardica's council in 343 for withdrawing his support. He was exiled to Upper Libya in Egypt, whence Julian's edict restoring banished bishops recalled him in 362. He joined Alexandria's council in 362, called partly to heal the Meletian schism troubling Antioch's church.

He was one bearer of that council's letter to the stubborn Lucifer of Cagliari and other bishops at Antioch. But Lucifer's haste in consecrating Paulinus as Meletius of Antioch's successor gave the schism new life and undid those peaceful measures. Asterius of Amasea in Pontus, about 400, is known only from a fact he himself relates, his education by a Scythian or Goth sent into his household.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atticus:
Atticus, born at Sebaste in Armenia, became Patriarch of Constantinople in 406 and held the see until his death in 425. Raised by Macedonian monks, he first shared their errors, then broke with them and rose to the priesthood. He accused St John Chrysostom at the Council of the Oak, which deposed the lawful patriarch in 405. He took the see after the death of his fellow intruder Arsacius.

At first he pressed the faithful to break from Chrysostom's communion, but they still shunned his services. He then restored his predecessor's name to the church diptychs, and charity to the poor slowly made him less hated. Pope Innocent I at last recognized him, though Rome later got his wider jurisdiction over Bithynia and Illyria recalled. Zeal for orthodoxy, against Messalians and Pelagians, partly made up for his irregular rise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aubert-miraeu:
Aubert Miraeus, also called Aubert le Mire, was an ecclesiastical historian born at Brussels in 1573 who died at Antwerp in 1640. After study at Douai and Louvain, he became canon of Antwerp cathedral in 1608. He then served as almoner and librarian to Archduke Albert, and in 1624 became dean of the cathedral and vicar general. The entry calls him a tireless writer, credited with thirty-nine works on general, church, and monastic history.

His chief books include a world chronicle from Christ's birth to 1608, a survey of bishoprics across the world, and a church geography. His history of Belgian churches was later re-edited by Foppens in four volumes. His Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica gathered short lives of church writers from Jerome to Henry of Ghent. He also wrote separate histories of the Benedictines, Carthusians, Carmelites, and other orders. On the whole he counts as reliable, though some works lack depth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustus:
Augustus is the name by which Caius Julius Caesar Octavianus, the first Roman emperor, is known. He was born at Rome in 62 BC and died in AD 14, and Jesus Christ was born during his reign. Augustus was a Senate title from 27 BC, given in thanks for restored privileges, and later emperors took the name. He belonged to the Octavian clan, was a praetor's son, and stood as grand-nephew and chief heir of Julius Caesar.

After Caesar's murder he went to Rome to claim his inheritance, first sided with the republicans, then allied with Mark Antony. Against the Senate's will he won the consulate in 43 BC and joined Antony and Lepidus in the Second Triumvirate for five years. Their first joint stroke crushed Caesar's murderers under Brutus and Cassius at Philippi in 42 BC. The entry ends with his census of Syria and Judaea under Quirinius, vital for dating Christ's birth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aurelius:
Aurelius was Archbishop of Carthage from 388 to 423, holding one of Christendom's foremost sees. Though not formally called Primate, Carthage's bishop confirmed episcopal nominations, presided over yearly plenary councils, and signed synodal letters for all. Aurelius held the post when Africa led the Church in intellect. His episcopate faced two great crises: the Donatists' last effort for a losing cause, and the first appearance of Pelagianism. He met both with wisdom.

Peace-loving, he treated repentant Donatists with indulgence in his synods, until their rebellion and murders drove him to join appeals to the secular power. He was the first to unmask Pelagianism, excommunicating Caelestius, Pelagius's disciple, in 412. In 416 a synod of sixty-eight bishops condemned both men, and Innocent I defined the need for grace and infant baptism. When Pope Zosimus was deceived by Pelagius, Aurelius warned him through a council in 417, and Zosimus condemned the heresiarchs in 418.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aurelius-clem:
Aurelius Clemens Prudentius was a Christian poet born in northern Spain in 348, who died there probably after 405. His birthplace is uncertain: Saragossa, Tarragona, or Calahorra. He practiced law with success, served twice as provincial governor, and was summoned to the emperor's court. Late in life he gave up the world's vanities for strict asceticism, fasting until evening and eating no animal food. His Christian poems belong to that late period, and he collected them with a preface dated 405.

His works divide three ways: lyrical, didactic, and polemical. The lyrical pieces form two collections, above all the Cathemerinon, hymns that sanctify the hours of the day and feasts such as Christmas and Epiphany. Some follow the liturgical tradition of St Ambrose. A trip to Rome about 403 let him visit martyrs' tombs, and poems of the Peristephanon followed that journey. His Contra Symmachum, written at Rome, defends the faith against pagan revival.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-azotus:
Azotus, Hebrew Ashdod and Esdud, was one of the five cities of the Philistines, near the Mediterranean between Gaza and Jaffa. Its temple of Dagon held the Ark of the Covenant after the Philistines captured it, as First Samuel tells. Like other Philistine cities, it suffered in wars with Israel, Assyria, and Egypt. Uzziah fought it, Sargon and Sennacherib took it, and Herodotus credits Psammetichus with a siege of twenty years in one part of the entry and twenty-nine in another.

In 163 BC Judas Machabeus cleared Azotus of idols, and in 148 BC Jonathan and Simon burned Dagon's temple. Today Esdud is a village whose ruins attest its past, and the New Testament mentions Azotus in Philip's return. The entry adds a second Azotus, the mountain where Bacchides pursued the Jews. It also lists a titular see of Palestine, from 325 to 536, the Ashdod of Joshua and seat of Dagon worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bacchylus:
Bacchylus was Bishop of Corinth, whom Eusebius counts among the churchmen. He is known only for backing Pope Victor I in the Quartodeciman controversy. That dispute turned on Easter's date, with the Asiatics keeping the Jewish fourteenth day against Rome's Sunday observance. When Victor, set on winning universal acceptance for the Roman paschal reckoning, wrote to win the support of influential churches, many synods met. Their bishops wrote back, all but the Asiatics in his favor.

Among them was Bacchylus, who by a ninth-century witness held a synod about 195 with eighteen other bishops. St Jerome attests that his letter, praised as elegant, was written in the name of the bishops of Achaia. Eusebius, who may have seen the letter, sets it apart from synodal letters, saying Bacchylus wrote alone. Perhaps he held a synod yet wrote personally, but no text survives, and the sources cited hold the only data.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bachiarius:
Bachiarius was an early fifth-century writer known only through two treatises. Those writings suggest a monk, possibly an abbot, from Spain. The first, called Liber de Fide by Gennadius, is an apologetical letter to the pope. Like other Spanish monks reaching Rome, he defended his faith against suspicion of Priscillian heresy. He said he left his country because of its errors, and some read that as exile.

His profession of faith in that letter witnesses to thorough orthodoxy. The second work, Ad Januariam, asks Abbot Januarius to soften severity toward a repentant, incontinent monk. That monk, though penitent, stood excluded from the monastery. The letter breathes a prudent, tempered charity, rich in scriptural texts and allusions. The theory that Bachiarius was Bishop Peregrinus of Spain seems untenable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baius:
Baius, or Michel de Bay, was a theologian and author of the system called Baianism. He was born at Melun in Hainaut in 1513 and died at Louvain in 1589. Though poor, he completed humanities, philosophy, and theology across Louvain's colleges. After ordination he became principal of Standonk College in 1541, then held the philosophy chair until 1550.

In 1550 he took his doctorate in theology and rose to the Scripture professorship within two years. With his friend John Hessels, he used the Trent absence of Louvain's leaders to spread new methods and doctrines. Chancellor Tapper, back from Trent in 1552, sought Cardinal Granvelle's help, which quieted the innovators for a time. After Tapper died in 1559, fresh trouble followed, and the Sorbonne censured eighteen propositions of Baius and Hessels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bar-hebraeus:
Bar Hebraeus, or Abu'l Faraj, was a Jacobite Syrian bishop, philosopher, poet, grammarian, physician, commentator, historian, and theologian. Born at Meletine in 1226, he died at Maragha in Persia in 1286. His father Aaron, a Jewish physician turned Jacobite, gave him the surname Bar 'Ebraya, 'Son of the Hebrew.' From boyhood he studied medicine and many branches of knowledge at Antioch and Tripoli, never abandoning study until death.

He became Bishop of Gubos in 1246, moved to Lacabene in 1247, took Aleppo in 1252, and rose to Primate of the East in 1264. His visitations across a vast province let him consult libraries and learned men wherever he traveled. Despite the Mongol invasion's upheavals, he amassed immense erudition across secular and religious knowledge. His main claim rests less on original work than on preserving and systematizing his predecessors' labors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barjesus: Barjesus was a false prophet found with Proconsul Sergius Paulus at Paphos in Cyprus, when Paul and Barnabas visited. Because he opposed the proconsul's conversion to Christianity, Paul struck him blind. He was also called Elymos, from Arabic 'alim, meaning wise, which Luke renders as magician. His story is told in Acts, where his blindness answers his resistance to the Gospel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barthold-nihu:
Barthold Nihus was a convert and controversialist, born at Holtorf in Hanover in 1590, who died at Erfurt in 1657. From a poor Protestant family, he studied philosophy and medicine at Helmstedt from 1607, serving as famulus to Professor Cornelius Martini. Master of philosophy in 1612, he turned to Protestant theology, then taught at Jena and tutored Saxe-Weimar's young princes. Protestant theologians' failure to agree on vital questions first made him doubt, then renounce Protestantism.

At Cologne in 1622 he entered the House of Proselytes, accepted the Catholic faith, and was ordained priest. He directed that house, became provost at Althaldensleben in 1627, and abbot of a Premonstratensian monastery two years later. Expelled after Breitenfeld in 1631, he fled to Hildesheim, then Holland, where he grew close to Vossius. With Leo Allatius he researched Greek Communion and liturgy and edited Allatius's works with valuable additions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomaeus:
Bartholomaeus Anglicus was a thirteenth-century Franciscan encyclopedist, English by birth. A Paris theology professor, he entered St Francis's order in 1224 or 1225 with Haymo of Faversham and two fellow professors. He lectured in the cloister school until 1231, when he was sent to Magdeburg in Germany. His death date is unknown, and he must not be confused with the later Bartholomaeus of Glanvilla, who died about 1360.

His De proprietatibus rerum, in nineteen books, encyclopedias the sciences of his age, from theology and medicine to zoology and mineralogy. It was the Middle Ages' first important encyclopedia and the first to draw on newly translated Greek, Arabian, and Jewish naturalists. At least fourteen editions appeared before 1500, with translations into French, Belgian, English, and Spanish. Through translation it shaped medieval thought more than Vincent's work, and it remains a valuable medieval source.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomew-m:
Bartholomew Mastrius was a Franciscan philosopher and theologian, born at Meldola, Italy, in 1602, who died in 1673. Educated at Cesena and Bologna, with time at Padua and Rome, he mastered scholastic philosophy and theology, steeped in Scotus. An open-minded, independent scholar, he was also a harsh controversialist, mixing invective with argument. His views drew fierce combat from Matthew Ferchi and the Irish Franciscan John Ponce.

Presenting his Sentences commentary to Alexander VII, he was asked where he learned to treat Ferchi so roughly. He answered, from Augustine and Jerome, who fought hard over Scripture's meaning, and the pope smilingly replied that other lessons could be learned from such masters. His arguments, for and against, show real critical power in clear, precise language. His five-volume Philosophy, four-volume Sentences commentaries, and one-volume Moral Theology all appeared at Venice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolomeo-eu:
Bartolomeo Eustachius was a Renaissance anatomist, born at San Severino in Italy early in the sixteenth century, who died at Rome in 1574. Hirsch calls him one of the greatest anatomists who ever lived. Well schooled in Latin, Greek, and Arabic, he took his medical degree and devoted himself to anatomy. With Vesalius and Columbus, he forms the trio who remade anatomy for modern times.

He served as physician to Cardinals Borromeo and della Rovere, and after Columbus's death became anatomy professor at the Sapienza. There he published works adding markedly to knowledge of most organs' structure. His neurology of the cranial nerves was especially full, and his account of foetal circulation was the most complete of his time. The valve guiding blood through the foramen ovale still bears his name as the Eustachian valve.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolommeo-g:
Bartolommeo Gavantus was a Barnabite liturgist born at Monza in 1569, who died at Milan in 1638. Early devoted to liturgical study, he won Roman fame as a most accurate knower of the sacred rites. His chief work, the Thesaurus sacrorum rituum of 1628, comments on the rubrics of the Roman Missal and Breviary.

It traces each rite's historical origin and mystical meaning, gives rules for observing the rubrics, and adds decrees and explanations. Cardinals Millino, Muto, and Cajetan approved it, and it was dedicated to Urban VIII. Gavantus became general of his order, and Urban named him perpetual consultor to the Congregation of Rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bassianus:
Bassianus was Bishop of Ephesus from 444 to 448. As a priest, his gifts to the poor won the people's love, and his jealous bishop Mennon tried to remove him by promoting him to Evaza. Bassianus spurned the forced rite, a stand Mennon's heir Basil backed. On Basil's death in 444, popular cheers swept Bassianus to the see despite church rules, and Theodosius II confirmed the election.

He ruled in peace for four years until a mob seized and jailed him at Easter 448. Pope Leo I with Constantinople, Alexandria, and Antioch voided his vote. Stephen, whom Bassianus called his foes' chief, replaced him. Chalcedon in 451, though keen to restore him, left the see open, retiring both men on pay with bishops' rank.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedictus-ar:
Benedictus Arias Montanus, a Spanish Orientalist and Bible editor, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Frejenal de la Sierra in 1527, he died at Seville in 1598 after study at Seville and Alcalá in theology and Eastern languages. Travel widened his command of European tongues, and he attended the Council of Trent in 1562 with the Bishop of Segovia.

King Philip II called him from a hermitage in 1568 to supervise a new polyglot Bible, a Bible printed in several languages side by side. Issued from the Plantin press at Antwerp with many learned helpers, it became his life's monument. The entry presents a scholar-monk trusted by king and council alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedictus-po: Benedictus Polonus was a medieval Franciscan missionary and traveller, companion of Giovanni da Pian del Carpine on the first Franciscan mission to the Tatars about 1245. His brief chronicle of the journey survives as a short report, valued above all for the letter of the Great Khan to Pope Innocent IV that it preserves. First printed in 1839, it was unknown to the order's early literary historians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berosus:
Berosus, a Babylonian priest and historian, is the subject of this long 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. A priest of Bel-Marduk, he lived in Alexander the Great's lifetime and at least into the reign of Antiochus I, to whom he dedicated his history of Babylonia. His name's meaning remains uncertain, despite fanciful guesses.

His Babyloniaca, written in Greek in three books, runs from the world's beginning to the Flood, then to Nabonassar in 747 BC, then to Alexander and Antiochus. He claims temple chronicles and inscriptions as sources, a claim the entry finds largely sound. Fragments preserved by later writers keep his Babylonian past alive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bisomus: Bisomus is a tomb large enough for two bodies in the Roman catacombs. Ordinary graves, called loci, held one body, but sometimes a space for two was cut, and inscriptions call it a locus bisomus. One inscription from St. Callistus tells of Boniface, dead at twenty-three years and two months, laid in a double grave prepared for himself and his father.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-bapti:
Blessed Baptista Mantuanus, also called Spagnoli, a Carmelite and Renaissance poet, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Mantua in 1447, eldest son of a Spanish nobleman at the Mantuan court, he died there in 1516. Schooling in grammar with Gregorio Tifernate, then philosophy at Pavia, shaped a youth led astray by schoolfellows, usurers, and a father's anger.

Turned out of his father's house, he went to Venice and Ferrara and entered the Carmelite convent of the Mantuan reform. His Latin eclogues and poems won fame across Europe, and he later served as vicar-general of his congregation. The entry presents a poet-monk of the Renaissance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-john-:
Blessed John Duns Scotus, surnamed the Subtle Doctor, is the subject of this long 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Founder of the Scotist school, chiefly among Franciscans, he died on 8 November 1308, probably born about 1270. Contemporary sources say little certain of his life, and his birthplace remains disputed, with Scotland the likeliest home.

A Merton College manuscript tying him to Oxford is dismissed, since college statutes barred monks and Scotus joined the Franciscans young. His subtle distinctions on being, individuation, and Mary's Immaculate Conception shaped Franciscan thought for centuries. The entry presents a thinker known by his system more than his biography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-mauru:
Maurus Magnentius Rabanus, abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz, made Fulda the most famous school in the Frankish Empire. He also wrote widely on theology and teaching. Born at Mainz about 776, he took Benedictine vows young and studied under Alcuin at Tours. He then returned to teach and lead Fulda's school.

Elected abbot in 822, he built more than thirty churches and enriched the abbey. He cared for preaching and country priests, and sided with Louis the Pious in the empire's civil wars. Forced to resign in 842, he retired to write. Reconciled with Louis the German, he became Archbishop of Mainz in 847 and held three synods on church discipline before his death in 856.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-peter:
Peter Igneus, the Fire-tried monk, earned his name by walking through fire to prove a charge of simony, the buying of church office, against the Bishop of Florence. An Italian Vallombrosian monk also called Peter Aldobrandini, he was chosen by Saint John Gualbert for the ordeal in 1068 and passed it, forcing the bishop's confession.

He later rose to abbot, then to Cardinal-Bishop of Albano in 1074, serving Gregory VII on delicate missions. In 1079 he went to Germany as papal legate to mediate between Henry IV and Rudolf of Swabia, and in 1084 he carried the renewed excommunication of Henry into France. He died in February 1089.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blossius-aemi:
Blossius Aemilius Dracontius, a Christian poet of fifth-century Carthage, wrote prison poems of faith after a life of wealth and law. From a distinguished family, he studied under the grammarian Felicianus and won favor with the proconsul Pacideius. His Romano-Byzantine sympathies angered the Vandal king Gunthamund, who jailed him for years.

His Romulea gathers rhetorical school pieces, including a rich man who claims a poor man's head and Achilles weighing whether to sell Hector's body. Prison produced his two Christian works: the Satisfactio of about 490, seeking royal pardon, and De laudibus Dei, praising God's benefits across creation, Incarnation, and Christian hope against pagan despair.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boethius:
