Boethius, Roman statesman and philosopher called the last of the Romans, wrote the Consolation of Philosophy in prison before his execution in 524 or 525. Born at Rome in 480 to a consular family, he was raised by Symmachus and married his daughter Rusticana. By 507 he served King Theodoric on important missions and enjoyed the king's trust.

Enemies accused him of plotting to restore Roman liberty and of sacrilege through astrology. Condemned unheard, he reflected in prison on the fickleness of princes and friends, and that reflection shaped his famous dialogue. Tradition honored him as a martyr, though the Consolation never names Christ. Scholars now hold from his theological tracts that he stayed Christian to the end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boleslaus-bal:
Boleslaus Balbinus, a Jesuit historian of Bohemia, spent his life gathering and editing his homeland's past. Born at Koniggratz on 4 December 1621 to an old noble family, he died at Prague in 1688. He wrote more than thirty works, and the Bollandists often drew on his research.

His chief work, the Miscellanea Historica regni Bohemiae in six volumes from 1679 to 1687, covers Bohemia's great events and the lives of its notable people. He also defended the Slavic and Bohemian tongue in Latin and wrote on Bohemia's archbishops. He first edited the old vernacular Life of Saint Ludmilla and Martyrdom of Saint Wenceslas, judged a tenth-century text.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bonino-mombri:
Bonino Mombritius, a Milanese humanist and editor, preserved ancient writings and saints' lives for Renaissance readers. Born in 1424 to a noble but modest Milan family, he studied Latin and Greek at Ferrara and taught Latin at Milan. Contemporaries praised both his learning and his earnest religious life, though misfortune dogged him without slowing his work.

His editions include chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome, the Scriptores rei Augustae, Papias's Glossary, and Solinus's Mirabilia mundi. His great hagiographic work, the Sanctuarium, gathered martyrdoms and lives of saints in two folio volumes, probably printed in 1480 and newly edited by the Solesmes Benedictines in 1910. He also wrote poems, among them De passione Domini. He died between 1482 and 1502.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bonosus:
Bonosus, Bishop of Sardica, taught that Mary bore other children after Jesus, against the Church's teaching on her perpetual virginity. The Council of Capua in 391 passed no judgment, but referred the case to Anysius of Thessalonica and the Illyrian bishops. They condemned him and tried to bar him from his church, and Pope Siricius approved the sentence.

Bonosus kept acting as bishop anyway, consecrating bishops and ordaining priests despite Ambrose's advice to submit. Innocent I later ruled that men he ordained before condemnation stood without reordination, while those ordained after it lost their rank. He died around the turn of the fifth century. His followers, the Bonosians, also denied Christ's divinity, holding only an adoptive sonship, and their baptisms divided opinion on validity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brothers-of-t:
The Brothers of the Cross of Jesus, founded at Lyons in 1820 by Father C. M. Bochard of the Sorbonne, take their spirit from the cross itself. Bochard served as first superior general until 1834, followed by Corsiain to 1865 and Bernard to 1874. Until then fathers of the congregation ran the chief houses, but in 1873 Bishop Richard of Belley set them as parish priests, and the body became brothers only.

The congregation grew through eastern France and Switzerland until the persecution of 1903 wrecked nearly all its houses. Superior General Firmin sent Brother Evariste with thirty-two religious to found a North American province under Bishop Blais of Rimouski. Quebec's legislature incorporated it in May 1905, and it opened a house of formation at Rimouski plus colleges at Saint-Jean-Baptiste and Saint-Pierre in Manitoba from 1904.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cadalous:
Cadalous, Bishop of Parma and antipope, was born of noble stock near Verona and died at Parma in 1072. After Nicholas II died in 1061, the cardinals under Hildebrand duly elected Alexander II. Twenty-eight days later an assembly at Basle, called by Empress Agnes, chose Cadalous, who took the name Honorius II. In spring 1062 he marched on Rome and seized the precincts of Saint Peter's, until Godfrey of Tuscany forced him back to Parma.

The new German regent Anno had Burchard of Halberstadt judge Alexander's election, and Alexander was upheld while Cadalous was excommunicated in 1063. Cadalous answered with his own ban, held Sant' Angelo for over a year, and fled to Parma as his cause failed. The Council of Mantua in 1064 anathematized him and declared Alexander the lawful successor of Saint Peter, yet Cadalous kept his claim until death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caius-marius-:
Caius Marius Victorinus, also called Victorinus Afer, was born in Africa about 300, a grammarian, rhetorician, philosopher, and theologian of the fourth century. As a teacher of rhetoric at Rome he won such fame that a statue rose to him in the Forum of Trajan in 353. Augustine calls him a man of supreme learning, thoroughly skilled in the liberal arts, and he wrote or translated many works.

Three pre-conversion works survive: a book of definitions, a commentary on Cicero's De Inventione, and a grammar. His conversion, before 361, came through study of the Bible, and he insisted on professing his faith as publicly as possible. He kept teaching until Julian's edict of 362 barred Christians from teaching, and his later Christian writings include works against Arianism and commentaries on Paul's letters to the Galatians, Ephesians, and Philippians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caius-valeriu:
Maximinus, nephew of Galerius, ruled Syria and Egypt as Caesar from 305 and took the title Augustus in 307, following Constantine's example. On Galerius's death in 311 he won the eastern provinces by remitting taxes, and an agreement fixed the Aegean and the straits as the border with Licinius, leaving three lawful emperors. A fanatical idolater, he pressed the persecution of Christians with special severity even where Galerius had eased it.

He also built a pagan priesthood to rival the Christian Church, ranking high priests and magicians with provincial governors. When Constantine and Licinius issued the Milan edict of toleration in 312, he published it only under pressure. Marching on Byzantium, he lost to Licinius near Adrianople on 30 April 313, fled to the Taurus, and took poison as his cause collapsed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-callinicus:
Callinicus in Asia Minor began as Nicephorium, founded by Alexander the Great, and took its name from Seleucus Callinicus, King of Syria from 246 to 225 B.C., who restored it. Emperor Leo I refortified it in the fifth century, after which Byzantine writers also called it Leontopolis. Two famous battles were fought on its broad plain, in 531 between Belisarius and the Persians and in 583 between Persians and Mauritius.

Callinicus answered to Edessa as suffragan. Lequien names four bishops, among them Paul, deposed in 519 as a Monophysite, whom the Jacobites call the interpreter of books for his many Syriac translations. The Syrian patriarch Michael lists twenty Jacobite bishops from the eighth to the thirteenth century. Today it is Raqqah near the Euphrates, a town of about 2,000 tents amid camel and horse pastures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-camachus:
Camachus was a titular see in Armenia, whose true early name seems to have been Camacha, with Camachus and Camache as later forms. It does not appear in church history before the seventh century. In 681 George, Bishop of Daranalis or Camachus, attended the Council of Constantinople, and in 692 he signed the acts of the Trullan Council.

Late in the ninth century Leo the Philosopher raised Camachus, till then suffragan of Sebaste, to a metropolis with five, at one time eight, suffragans. Bishop Sisinnius appears in 1028, and by the fifteenth century the see had vanished. Today it is Kemakh on the western Euphrates, a town trading in gloves and carpets amid old Byzantine and Turkish castles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-candidus:
Candidus is the name of two scholars of the Carolingian revival in the ninth century. The first, Candidus Bruun of Fulda, learned from Abbot Aegil. Abbot Ratger sent him to Einhard at Charlemagne's court, where he likely learned the art he used to paint the apse that received Saint Boniface's remains in 819. Under Rabanus Maurus he headed Fulda's monastic school.

As a philosopher he is known for twelve aphoristic sayings on the image of God, drawn from Saint Augustine. The last saying makes the Middle Ages' first timid attempt at a proof of God's existence, close kin to Anselm's ontological argument. The second Candidus is Wizo, the Anglo-Saxon scholar Alcuin renamed, who tutored Charlemagne's sister and daughter and succeeded Alcuin as master of the palace school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canopus:
Canopus was an Egyptian city and titular see, known to Egyptians as Pikuat and to Greeks as Kanobos. The Greek name recalls a fleet commander buried there. It stood near the Canopic mouth of the Nile. Under Diocletian it gathered martyrs, including Athanasia with her three daughters and Cyrus and John. Its monastery of Metanoia sheltered Alexandrian patriarchs during fifth-century religious quarrels.

Two miles east stood a famed pagan temple, later replaced by a church for the Evangelists. Cyril of Alexandria placed the relics of Cyrus and John there. Sophronius of Jerusalem, healed of an eye ailment judged incurable, wrote a praise of the saints with seventy miracles. The entry closes with the later town, its quail trade, and the battles off Aboukir in 1798, 1799, and 1801.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carystus:
Carystus was a titular see of Greece, named by legend after Carystus, a son of Chiron. Geographers mention the ancient city chiefly for its fine marble and its amianth from Mount Oche. At first a suffragan of Corinth, it passed early in the ninth century to Athens and before 1579 to Euripos, or Chalcis.

Lequien names only two Greek bishops: Cyriacus, who signed the bishops' letter to Emperor Leo in 458, and Joel early in the eighteenth century. Demetrius, friend of the Athenian metropolitan Michael Acominatos, counts as another titular. Kept in 1833 under the name Carystia with its titular at Kyme, it joined Chalcis in 1900. Today it is a village of about 2,000 people on the southern coast of Euboea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cassiodorus:
Cassiodorus, in full Flavius Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator, was a Roman writer, statesman, and monk born about 490 who died about 583. Of Syrian ancestry, his family ranked among the most important in Bruttium for three generations. His great-grandfather defended the region in the Vandal invasion of 455, and his father rose to praetorian prefect and patrician under Theodoric. Born at Scyllaceum, he served as councillor to the praetorian prefect about 501.

A panegyric on Theodoric won him the quaestorship between 507 and 511 and the consulship in 514. He became minister in 526, the year Theodoric died, with influence lasting through Amalaswintha's regency. In retirement he built Vivarium monastery on his own estate, where he kept writing past ninety-three. His Institutiones, written between 543 and 555 to give monks tools for reading Scripture, set out a course of study far beyond simple Bible meditation. The entry also weighs his influence on church music.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caunus:
Caunus, or Kaunos, was a titular see of Asia Minor. Legend names Kaunos, son of Miletos and Kyane, as its founder, across from Rhodes on Caria's southern shore. Called Rhodian Peraea, it lay below Mount Tarbelos. It exported prized figs chiefly to Rome. The painter Protogenes came from there. Its acropolis bore the name Imbros.

Church lists still place Caunus in Lycia, as a suffragan of Myra, into the twelfth or thirteenth century. Lequien names four bishops. Basil attended Seleucia's council in 359, and Antipater was present at Chalcedon in 451. Nicolaus signed the letter to Emperor Leo in 458, and Stephanus attended Nicaea in 787. The city's ruins, including a theatre, a probable temple, a Byzantine church, and rock-hewn tombs, lie near the modern village of Dalian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-census:
Census is a canonical term defined in several ways by different writers. Zitelli describes it as a real obligation, an annual tribute that a bishop lays on a pious institute, payable to himself or others. Aicher calls it an offering from a benefice marking subjection, or given for some exemption or right granted to it.

Laurentius defines it as a yearly payment in money or kind, laid on a benefice for good. Ferraris treats census as the right of drawing an annual payment from something fruitful on which it is founded, not the property itself. Other authorities view it as the property or its money equivalent. Census must be distinguished from pensio, the right a superior grants someone to a share of a benefice's revenues held by a third party.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ceramus:
Ceramus, also spelled Keramos, was a Carian city, at first subject to Stratonicea and afterwards autonomous. It ranked among the chief cities of the Systema Chrysaorikon. Under Rome it struck its own coinage. It appears in the Notitiae episcopatuum into the twelfth or thirteenth century, listed under Aphrodisias, also called Stauropolis.

Only three bishops are known. Spudasius attended Ephesus in 431, Maurianus attended Nicaea in 787, and Symeon attended the council that reinstated Photius in 879. Ceramus has kept its old name. It is today just a small village in Smyrna's vilayet, on the Keramic Gulf's north shore, near the sea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cerasus:
Cerasus was a titular see in Pontus Polemoniacus, Asia Minor, remembered for Xenophon's stay with his Ten Thousand during their famous retreat. The town seems to have stood in the valley a short distance from the modern city, which Pharnaces founded and named Pharnacia after himself. Cherry trees grew so thickly in the country that it soon took the name Cerasus, like the old town, and the name has remained.

Pompey brought the first cherry trees to Rome from Cerasus, and from there they spread through all Europe. The city was a suffragan of Neocaesarea. It became a metropolis in the eleventh century and survived to the end of the fifteenth, though the see was suppressed by the seventeenth. Its modern successor, Kerassoun or Ghiresson, is a Black Sea port of about 10,000 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cerinthus:
Cerinthus was a heretic of Gnostic-Ebionite stamp, living in St. John's time. The Fourth Gospel is said to have been written against his errors on the divinity of Christ. No information about this early sectary survives from his own times. Irenaeus gives the first mention of his name and doctrines, written about 170. Further matter comes from Presbyter Caius around 210 as quoted by Eusebius, and from Hippolytus around 230, who largely transcribes Irenaeus.

Later witnesses include Pseudo-Tertullian about 240 and a fragment of Dionysius of Alexandria about 250. The fullest account comes in Epiphanius about 390, which must be used with some caution given its date and character. Cerinthus was an Egyptian, circumcised if not a Jew by race, who founded a school in Asia and gathered disciples. His doctrines mixed Jewish and Gnostic elements, and no writings of his survive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charadrus:
Charadrus stood as a harbour and fortress in Cilicia Tracheia. It lay on the coast of Asia Minor between Anemurium and Antioch. Strabo and Skylax record it, and its Greek name lives on in Kalandran, a small village in the Adana region with about 280 people. Its bishop Nounechios attended the Council of Chalcedon in 451. In 458 he signed the Isaurian bishops' letter to Emperor Leo under the double title of Lamos and Charadrus.

That pairing shows Charadrus was joined early to Lamos. Lamos was a see in Isauria under Seleuceia. No later bishops are recorded, and the union with Lamos remains the main fact of its history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chersonesus:
An entry on Chersonesus, a name borne by two titular sees, bishoprics kept in name. The first, in Crete, stood on a small peninsula between Cnossus and Olous on the north-east coast and served as the seaport of Lyttos. Known in the fourth century before Christ for its temple of Britomartis, it appears in Church lists with four Greek bishops from 441 to 789. Seven Latin bishops followed from 1298 to 1549.

The last two Latin bishops of the Cretan see, Dionysius and Joannes Franciscus Verdura, attended the Council of Trent. A later bishop, Pietro Coletti, appears early in the seventeenth century, though whether he belonged to the Greek or the Latin rite is unknown. The second Chersonesus, in Thrace and suffragan to Heracleia, lay near Callipolis, now Gallipoli, with one Greek bishop named in 449 and one Latin bishop in 1527. Its ruins near modern Khersonisi mark the Cretan site.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-lup:
An entry on Christian Lupus, the Augustinian historian whose surname means Wolf, born at Ypres in July 1612. He joined the Augustinians at fifteen, lectured in theology at Cologne, and won the trust of the nuncio Fabio Chigi, later Alexander the Seventh. Made professor at Louvain in 1640, he was suspected of Jansenism for his zeal for Saint Augustine, and the Brussels nuncio blocked his doctorate until the pope intervened.

Called to Rome by Alexander the Seventh, Lupus spent five years under papal protection studying church history, back at Louvain in 1660, he won election as provincial of the Belgian province. In 1667 he went back to Rome with Louvain professors to seek censure of faulty moral doctrines, and Innocent the Eleventh condemned sixty-five propositions he had denounced. His writings, published in thirteen parts, hold detailed council histories with learned dissertations, plus replies to Quesnel, Boileau, and Gerbais.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-b:
An entry on Christopher Besoldus, a German jurist and publicist born of Protestant parents at Tübingen in 1577. He studied law, took his doctorate in 1598, and became professor of law at Tübingen in 1610, where his counsel was often sought by the civil administration. Beyond law he learned nine languages and read Scripture, the Fathers, and medieval mystics.

Besoldus was publicly received into the Church at Heilbronn in 1635, and two years later took the chair of Roman law at Ingolstadt. He was weighing a Bologna professorship offered by Urban the Eighth when he died in September 1638. On his deathbed he begged his wife to embrace the faith, and three months later she entered the Church with their eight-year-old daughter. His Stuttgart archive documents offended Württemberg by proving that monastic dependence on the empire bound dukes to restore seized church property.

An entry on Christopher Borrus, born at Milan in 1583, he was a missionary, mathematician, and astronomer. From a good Milanese family, he joined the Society of Jesus in September 1601. In 1616 he sailed from Macao with Father Marquez among the first missionaries to Cochin-China, where he stayed until 1622 under the name Bruno. Back home he taught mathematics at Coimbra, then in 1632 joined the Cistercians as Father Onofrio, dying the same year.

His Relation of the new mission to Cochin-China, printed at Rome in 1631, was translated into French, Dutch, Latin, German, and English. It counted among the best sources on the country for its account of physical, political, and church conditions. Borrus also studied the compass. Kircher credits him with the first chart of the Atlantic and Indian Oceans marking where the needle makes equal angles with the meridian, making him a forerunner of Halley.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-c:
An entry on Christopher Clavius, mathematician and astronomer, whose chief achievement was the reform of the calendar under Gregory the Thirteenth. Born at Bamberg in 1538, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1555, showed mathematical talent at Coimbra, and taught at the Collegium Romanum in Rome until his death in February 1612. Tycho Brahe, Kepler, Galileo, and Magini esteemed him, and he was called his century's Euclid.

Clavius issued his writings at Mainz in five folio volumes as his collected mathematical works. The first holds Euclid and the Sphere of Theodosius, the second practical geometry and algebra. The third holds a commentary on the Sphere of Sacrobosco with a treatise on the astrolabe. The fourth holds the fullest discussion of sundials of its day, and the fifth his calendar work. The entry clears away myths about him, including a cardinal's hat and death by a mad bull.

An entry on Christopher Columbus, the Genoese navigator born probably in 1451 and dead at Valladolid in May 1506. His family was respectable but poor, his schooling thin, and he went to sea young, learning navigation, astronomy, and cosmography from Ptolemy and Cardinal d'Ailly's Imago Mundi. Letters of 1474 from the Florentine physicist Toscanelli, whose genuineness has been attacked, fit his later course toward Asia by the west.

Sailing for Spain's sovereigns, Columbus landed in the Bahamas, naming the island San Salvador, then founded the first Spanish settlement on Santo Domingo, which he called Hispaniola, leaving some sixty men there. Later voyages took him to Cuba, Jamaica, and the mainland coasts, and a fourth voyage tested his belief in a direct passage to Asia. The entry weighs his seamanship, his writings, and his fame, setting the discoverer against the controversies that have gathered around his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chronicle-of-:
An entry on the Chronicle of Eusebius, a universal history in two parts brought down to the year 225. The first part, probably called the Chronograph, is an epitome of world history in five sections: Chaldeans and Assyrians with king lists, Old Testament history, Egyptian history, Greek history, and Roman history. It quotes freely from lost authors, and its Babylonian creation and flood stories, preserved through Berosus, remain its most prized survivals.

The second part, the Canons, sets out chronological tables with short historical notes, using the years of Abraham from his supposed birth as the backbone, with regnal years of kings alongside. The original is lost, but both parts survive in an Armenian version, translated by Zohrab and Aucher in 1818 and superseded by Schoene, while Jerome translated the Canons into Latin. Syriac epitomes and extracts in Syncellus add further witnesses to the text.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cidyessus:
A short entry on Cidyessus, a titular see of Asia Minor, a city of some importance in west-central Phrygia, west of Ammonia. It lay in the territory of the Setchanli Ova, the Mouse Plain, a large fertile valley reaching into Phrygia Salutaris, though the city itself belonged to Phrygia Pacatiana. An inscription at Ghieuktché Euyuk village, west of Afium Kara Hissar, fixed its site.

Coins read Kidyessos, though its old native name may have been Kydessos. Three bishops only are named by Lequien: Heraclius, Andreas, and Thomas, in 451, 787, and 879. The see still appears in later lists of bishoprics until the twelfth or thirteenth century as a suffragan of Laodicea. The entry rests on Radet in Phrygia and Ramsay's historical geography of Asia Minor, and it leaves the small Phrygian see plainly mapped.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cisamus:
Cisamus, a titular see of Crete, stood at Kisamos, a harbour on the north-west coast that served Aptera as its port. Lequien names two Greek bishops only, Theopemptus in 692 and Leo in 787; Gerasimus about 1500 comes from Gams. The see still exists, suffragan to Candia.

Under Venetian rule, a Latin see under Gortyna and Candia also existed. Lequien names ten Latin bishops from 1346 to 1589, and Eubel twenty from about 1305 to 1498. Angelo Barbadigo, made cardinal by the antipope Nicholas the Fifth, held Cisamus before moving to Verona. Kissamo Kasteli is now a small port used only by coasting boats.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claudianus-ma:
Claudianus Mamertus, a Gallo-Roman theologian and brother of Saint Mamertus, Bishop of Vienne, died about 473. Probably sprung from a leading family, he gave up worldly goods for monastic life and helped his brother in his duties. Sidonius Apollinaris describes him directing the chanters' psalm-singing in alternating groups while the bishop celebrated at the altar. The passage matters for the history of liturgical chant. Sidonius also credits him with a lectionary of Scripture readings for feasts.

His treatise On the State of the Soul, written between 468 and 472, answered Faustus of Riez on whether the soul is bodily. Plato, Porphyry, Plotinus, and Saint Augustine supplied his arguments. His method, however, followed Aristotle and foreshadowed the Schoolmen. His language shared that character, using many abstract adverbs and reviving obsolete words. A letter to the rhetorician Sapaudus sanctioned imitating Naevius, Plautus, Varro, and Gracchus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claudius-clav:
Claudius Clavus, the Latin form of Claudius Clausson Swart, an old Danish cartographer, was born at Salling on Fünen on 14 September 1388. He made the first map of North-Western Europe, including the first map of Greenland. On journeys to Italy he stirred Rome's Humanists in 1424. He reported three volumes of Livy's Ten Decades seen at Soroe monastery, whose chapter titles he claimed to have read.

Through the Humanists he learned Ptolemy's maps. He set out to supplement them with a North-West chart and description. His first such drawing and description survive in the Ptolemy manuscript of 1427 belonging to Cardinal Fillastre, now at Nancy. It places Greenland and Iceland correctly west of Scandinavia. A second map and description matters still more for cartography. It survives only through the German cartographers Donnus Nicholas Germanus and Henricus Martellus Germanus at Florence, and no copy holds both map and text.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cocussus:
Cocussus, a titular see of Armenia, was a Roman station on the Cilicia to Caesarea road, first in Cappadocia, later in Armenia Secunda. Saint Paul the Confessor was exiled there and put to death by Arians in 350. It was also Saint John Chrysostom's exile, banished by Arcadius. His journey lasted seventeen days. The bishop and Dioscurus received him kindly. He lived three years at Cocussus, from 404 to 407.

The panegyric of Saint Gregory, attributed to Chrysostom, is not authentic, though an Armenian text of 1877 may be genuine. Cocussus appears in Hierocles's Synecdemus and in bishopric lists as late as the twelfth century, suffragan to Melitene. At Chalcedon in 451 Domnus was represented; Longinus subscribed the Armenian Secunda letter to Emperor Leo in 458, and Johns subscribed at Constantinople in 553 and at Trullan in 692. Armenian bishops held it in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries; today it is Guksun and Kokison.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-codex-alexand:
Codex Alexandrinus, a valuable Greek Old and New Testament manuscript, takes its name from Alexandria, its patriarch's former property. It was the first great uncial known to the learned world. Cyril Lucar, moving in 1621 from Alexandria to Constantinople, is believed to have brought it with him.

Later, a present to King James the First was sent, but James died first, and Charles the First accepted it in 1627. The codex holds the Bible of the Catholic canon, including deuterocanonical books, and joins to Machabees the apocryphal Third and Fourth Machabees. The New Testament adds the Epistle of Saint Clement of Rome and the homily passing as the Second Epistle of Clement. A prefixed list of New Testament books seems to rank them as Scripture, while Solomon's Psalms, now missing, were originally present yet set apart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-codex-amiatin:
Codex Amiatinus, the Latin Vulgate Bible's most celebrated manuscript, stands as the best witness to Saint Jerome's true text, now kept at Florence in the Laurentian Library. The immense tome measures 19 and a quarter inches by 13 and three-eighths and seven inches thick, impressive enough, Hort says, to fill the beholder with awe.

Its 1,029 leaves are strong, smooth vellum, fresh-looking today, arranged in quires of four sheets. Uncial characters, large, clear, and regular, run two columns to a page with 43 or 44 lines to a column. words are often separated by a little space, but the writing is continuous. There are no punctuation marks, but a stichometric arrangement into coda and commata guides the skilled reader into the sense. The scribe is believed to have modelled this manner on Cassiodorus's great Bible, though it may go back to Saint Jerome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-codex-ephraem:
Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus, symbol C, is the last of the four great uncials of the Greek Bible. It takes its name from treatises of Saint Ephraem the Syrian, translated into Greek, written over the original text in the twelfth century, after its ink had partly faded. Several biblical codices are palimpsests, and Ephraemi is the most important of them. After Constantinople's fall it reached Florence, then Paris through Catherine de Medici.

Torn leaves, faded ink, and the later covering made decipherment extremely difficult. Tischendorf, then young, won his reputation through the achievement, though his unchecked results demand caution. The codex, of good vellum, measures 12 and a quarter inches by nine, with one column to a page. Its writing runs a little larger than that of Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus, with no breathings or accents from the first hand and periods marked by a single point.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-codex-sinaiti:
Codex Sinaiticus, marked by the Hebrew character Aleph, is a Greek Old and New Testament manuscript of antiquity and value. Visiting in 1844 under Frederick Augustus, Tischendorf discovered forty-three leaves of the Septuagint in a rubbish basket, holding parts of First Paralipomenon, Jeremias, Nehemias, and Esther, and was allowed to take them.

He also saw Isaias and First and Fourth Machabees from the same codex but could not obtain them. He warned the monks of their value, left for Europe, and in 1846 published his leaves as Codex Friderico-Augustanus, now preserved at Leipzig. A third visit in 1859, under Czar Alexander the Second, seemed fruitless until, on departure's eve, the steward mentioned a manuscript. Shown it, Tischendorf found the codex he sought, holding much of the Old Testament, the entire New Testament, Barnabas, and the Shepherd of Hermas in part.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-codex-vatican:
Codex Vaticanus, or Codex B, is a Greek manuscript, most important of all Holy Scripture manuscripts. The quarto volume, written in fourth-century uncial letters on fine parchment bound in quinterns, divides each page into three columns of forty lines. In poetical books, stichometric division leaves two columns to a page.

Its first writer used neither pauses nor accents and rarely used simple punctuation. Unfortunately the codex is mutilated, with missing folios later replaced by others. The first twenty original folios are missing, with part of folio 178, ten folios after folio 348, and the final quinterns, whose number cannot be established. The Old Testament, in the Septuagint version except Daniel from Theodotion, fills 617 folios. Its gaps include Genesis 1 to 46:28, Second Samuel 2:5 to 7 and 10 to 13, and Psalms 105:27 to 137:6. The New Testament, beginning at folio 618, loses Hebrews 9:14 to 13:25, the Pastoral Letters, Philemon, and the Apocalypse through the missing final quinterns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cogitosus:
Edward D'Alton's entry treats Cogitosus, an Irish monk of Kildare. He wrote a life of Saint Brigid. His dates and his century are unknown. Some early writers read his plea for prayer as proof that he was Brigid's nephew. That reading would place him in the sixth century. His editor Vossius disagreed, since family lists of Brigid's kin never name him. Cogitosus also writes of a long line of later bishops and abbesses at Kildare.

Other clues push him later still. He calls Saint Conleth an archbishop, a title rare in the West before the ninth century. Yet he describes Kildare before Danish raiders plundered it in 835. His Latin is fairly good for the age. His picture of the church of Kildare, with its inner decoration, stays valuable for the history of early Irish art and building.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-columbus:
Lawrence Mulhane's entry covers the Diocese of Columbus in Ohio. It takes the part of the state south of 40 degrees 41 minutes, between the Ohio River east and the Scioto west, plus Delaware, Franklin, and Morrow counties. That is twenty-nine of Ohio's eighty-eight counties, with 13,685 square miles. The land once belonged to the Diocese of Cincinnati. Fathers of the Second Plenary Council of Baltimore in 1866 urged Rome to raise it as a see. Documents of 3 March 1868 did so, naming Sylvester Horton Rosecrans first bishop.

Early Columbus was farm country, settled from Pennsylvania and Maryland. Rosecrans died on 21 October 1878. By the time of writing the diocese counted 142 priests, 105 secular and 37 regular, with 34 brothers and 450 sisters. It had already given the Church two bishops, Fitzgerald of Little Rock and Gallagher of Galveston. The entry thus maps a young diocese growing on Ohio soil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commodianus:
Paul Lejay's entry follows Commodianus, a Christian poet of uncertain birth date. Most place him near the middle of the third century, or between Diocletian's persecution and Maxentius's edict. Some lately argued he lived under Julian, or even in the fifth century. Outside his own writings he is known only through Gennadius and Pseudo-Gelasius, who banned his books. Gennadius seems to draw his facts from the works themselves.

Two passages show Commodianus came from Gaza in Palestine and held episcopal rank. Gennadius claims he imitated Tertullian, Lactantius, and Papias. His works comprise a set of Instructions and a Carmen apologeticum, an apologetic poem. His sources ran from the Bible, above all the Apocalypse, the Prophets, and Fourth Esdras, to the Sibylline oracles and Latin fathers. Lejay weighs the dating dispute and leaves the poet's age open, with the fifth-century thesis marked very uncertain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commodus:
Patrick Healy's entry follows Marcus Aurelius Commodus Antoninus, Roman emperor born in 161 and dead at Rome on 31 December 192. Son of Marcus Aurelius and Faustina, he was the first emperor born in the purple, while his father reigned. His reign, from 180 to 193, marked a turning point in Rome's greatness. Some historians excuse him, blaming weak character and vicious friends. Healy stresses a deeper cause: his lack of capacity and evil life, joined to power long centered in the emperor.

Greed and suspicion marked his career, bringing confiscations and murders wholesale. One side effect eased the Christians' lot for a time. No edicts struck them, and proconsuls persecuted only in some provinces. Many Christians stood at court, and Marcia, the emperor's concubine or morganatic wife, won release for Christian prisoners from Sardinia's mines. Commodus died by strangling, with Marcia among the plotters. No evidence ties Christians to his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comte-de-cayl:
Louis Delamarre's entry follows Anne-Claude-Philippe de Tubières-Grimoard de Pestels de Lévis, Comte de Caylus, French archaeologist born at Paris in 1692, dead in 1765. Eldest son of a lieutenant-general, he learned much from his mother, whose Souvenirs enrich history. At seventeen he joined the army and fought in Spain and Germany. After the peace of Rastadt in 1714, he left war for arts and sciences. He traveled Italy, Greece, the East, England, and Germany, viewing ruins and gathering antiquities.

His zeal to verify ancient historians firsthand led him to hire highwaymen as guides at Ephesus and Colophon. Back in Paris he wrote his great Recueil d'antiquités, seven volumes from 1752 to 1767, two posthumous. With Mariette and others he built the Peintures antiques trouvées à Rome. Member of two academies, painter, engraver, and inventor of a marble inlay process, he wrote novels and fairy tales for leisure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concursus:
James David O'Neill's entry explains concursus, a special competitive examination in canon law for aspirants to offices carrying the cure of souls. For three hundred years no parish priests, strictly speaking, existed. One church in the bishop's city served town and country for Mass, teaching, and sacraments. Growth forced new churches, served by cathedral priests, so the cathedral stood as each diocese's only parish, with the bishop as chief pastor. Rural parishes grew on the same pattern.

New rules then opened benefices, above all major ones with parochial duties, to competition. Trent's regulations stand clear, though canonists debated whether neglect made appointments illicit or invalid. Appointments to erected parishes without concursus are null, unless long usage or special grant abrogated Trent's law. Baltimore's Third Plenary Council of 1884 ordered one parish in ten in each American diocese to become a permanent rectorship. Canada has none.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
William De Boeck's entry follows the Congregation of Picpus, formally the Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary and of Perpetual Adoration. Father Coudrin, born at Coursay-les-Bois in Poitou on 1 March 1768, founded it. A deacon when persecution scattered Poitiers students, he learned Clermont's Bishop de Bonald would ordain him in Paris. On 4 March 1792 the Irish Seminary ordained him in its library, revolutionaries having seized the chapel. Back at Coursay, violence forced hiding. Disguised, he labored in Poitiers and Tours that October.

Coudrin gathered companions to promote devotion to the Sacred Hearts. Pius VII in 1817, Leo XII in 1825, and Gregory XVI in 1840 approved it. In 1825 the Holy See entrusted Sandwich Islands evangelization to the congregation, with the first band sailing the next year. Houses and schools spread, with arts training at Louvain. England's superior sits at Eccleshall's Damien House, America's at Fairhaven's monastery in Massachusetts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-consentius:
Paul Lejay's entry treats Consentius, a fifth-century Gallo-Roman family with three known representatives. Consentius of Narbonne, Clarissimus, joined prefecture's honor with philosophy and corresponded with Sidonius Apollinaris, who dedicated him a Narbonne poem. He used every metre, iambic, elegiac, hendecasyllabic, hexameter, writing Greek and Latin. His poems breathe flowers and thyme, yet Sidonius's praises need care: he counted thirty similarly gifted friends. France's literary history distinguishes the dedicatee from the letter-writer, making the former father of the latter.

That father, Consentius of Narbonne, poet and contemporary of Valentinian, was Jovinus's son-in-law, consul in 367. A third Consentius, Gallic grammarian, wrote two treatises, perhaps fragments of a complete grammar: noun and verb, much used in the Carolingian period, and barbarisms and metaplasm. Keil published these treatises in his Grammatici Latini, volume five. Three lives under one name span poetry, letters, and grammar across fifth-century Gaul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-constantine-a:
James Joseph Walsh's entry follows Constantine Africanus, medical writer born about 1015, died about 1087. Africanus comes from his birthplace, Carthage. Early he gave himself to medicine, journeying to the Far East. He mastered Oriental languages and Arabian medicine, unknown in the West. Returning to Carthage, he met jealousy, even accusation of magic, and became secretary to Constantine Monomachus at Reggio.

At Salerno he taught medicine, drawing attention. After a few years he gave up honors and goods for Monte Cassino, welcomed by Desiderius, later Pope Victor III. Nearly twenty years there he wrote. His best-known work, Liber Pantegni, translates Ali Ben el-Abbas's Khitaab el Maleki, dedicated to Desiderius. Original works resist separation from attributions, leaving his contributions uncertain. With Constantine begins Salerno's second epoch, famed for translating Greek and Arabian writers and original work, with twelfth-century professors calling him master. Basle's 1536 folio stands as the chief edition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelius:
Florentine Bechtel's entry treats Cornelius, a centurion of the Italic cohort, converted at Cæsarea with his household in Acts 10. His Roman name suggests membership in the gens Cornelia, or descent from one of its freedmen, most likely the latter. His cohort was probably the Cohors II Italica, proved by a recent inscription stationed in Syria before A.D. 69.

Described as a religious man fearing God and giving alms to the people, that is, the Jews, Cornelius ranks among gentiles incorrectly called proselytes of the gate. The Church's gates, admitting thus far only the circumcised observing Moses's Law, now opened to uncircumcised Gentiles. Jerusalem's Jewish Christians disapproved, but opposition ceased when Peter related his and Cornelius's vision and the Holy Ghost's descent, except among a few extremists. One tradition makes him Bishop of Cæsarea, another Bishop of Scepsis in Mysia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corycus:
Siméon Vailhé's entry covers Corycus, a titular see of Cilicia Trachæa in Asia Minor. It served as Seleucia's port, where in 191 B.C. Romans defeated Antiochus the Great's fleet. In Roman times it kept its ancient laws, and emperors usually stationed a fleet there to watch pirates. Armenians soon conquered Corycus, holding it until the fourteenth century's middle, when Turks occupied it temporarily.

Peter I, King of Cyprus, captured it in 1361. From 1448 or 1454 it passed alternately to Karamanlis, Egyptians, Karamanlis again, and finally Osmanlis. Its ruins stand at Ghorghos, twenty-eight miles northeast of Selefke, Seleucia, in Adana's vilayet. Two medieval castles, one on the shore, one on an islet, joined by a ruined pier, stand partially preserved. Lequien mentions five Greek bishops from 381 to 680, one Latin bishop, Gerardus, and four more in the fourteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corydallus:
Sophrone Pétridès's entry covers Corydallus, a titular see, a bishopric kept in name only, of Asia Minor. Its older name was Korydallos, later also Korydalla, and it was a Lycian city. In Roman times the city struck coins. It appears in the Notitiæ episcopatuum, the lists of bishoprics, with entries running to the twelfth or thirteenth century, suffragan of Myra.

Lequien mentions only four bishops. Alexander is known only from a mention in Saint Basil's letter 218. Palladius appears in the years 451 and 458. Leo appears in 787, and Eustratius in 879. Corydallus has not yet been identified with any known site. A second see of the same name existed in Pamphylia, suffragan to Perge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-ep:
The Council of Ephesus, the third ecumenical council, met in 431 over the teaching of Nestorius, Bishop of Constantinople. Cyril of Alexandria had accused Nestorius of heresy before Pope Celestine, who ordered him to recant within ten days or face excommunication and deposition. Nestorius, feeling calumniated and unwilling to fall into Cyril's hands, sought a council instead.

Cyril opened proceedings on 22 June with some 160 bishops, rising to 198 by evening, and the council condemned Nestorius. Sessions continued into the autumn, with imperial letters, rival synods, and appeals complicating the record. Nestorius, anticipating his fate, asked leave to retire to his former monastery before the synod dissolved about early October.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crescentius:
This historical entry follows three leaders of the Roman aristocracy named Crescentius, who dominated Rome in the tenth century against emperors and popes. Crescentius the Elder rose from the family of Theophylactus, which controlled papal nominations and held power for years. In 974 he rebelled against Otto II, deposed Pope Benedict VI, and had him strangled in Sant' Angelo.

Crescentius the Younger took power after his father's death, ruling while Otto III was a child and clashing with the young emperor. His son John Crescentius led the revolt of 1001 that drove Otto III and Pope Sylvester II from Rome. With John's death in 1012, the Crescentii vanish from Roman history, and the entry draws on Duchesne and Gregorovius throughout.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cresconius:
A biographical entry presents Cresconius, also called Crisconius, a Latin canonist whose date and place are uncertain, probably a bishop of the African Church in the later seventh century. His work, the Concordia canonum, gathers the Apostolic Canons, nearly all fourth- and fifth-century council canons, and many papal decretals from the fourth and fifth centuries.

Its contents follow Dionysius Exiguus, while its division into 301 titles copies Fulgentius Ferrandus. A table of contents preceded the text in many manuscripts, and the whole work first appeared in print in 1661. Debate over a poem on an African victory has shifted his date between the sixth and eighth centuries. The Concordia served African and Gallic churches as a handy manual until the tenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cyprus:
A country entry describes Cyprus, an eastern Mediterranean island at the mouth of the Gulf of Alexandretta. First Phoenician and Greek, famed for temples of Aphrodite, it passed from Egyptians and Persians to Alexander, then Ptolemies, then Romans in 59 BC. Richard the Lion-Hearted conquered it in 1191 and gave it to Guy de Lusignan, and it passed through Genoese and Venetian hands before falling to the Turks in 1571. England occupied it in 1878.

Hilly and hot, with few rivers, it covers 3,584 square miles and counted 237,000 people in 1901, mostly Greeks, with Muslims, Maronites, Latins, and Armenians. It yields dates, carobs, oranges, oil, wine, corn, and sponges, and copper was mined in ancient times. Paul, Barnabas, and John Mark preached Christianity there, and the entry traces its churches through Lusignan, Venetian, and British rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cyrrhus:
A historical entry describes Cyrrhus, a titular see of Syria and capital of the district of Cyrrhestica between Antioch and Commagene. Its origin is unknown, though a sixth-century tale falsely derived it from Cyrus of Persia by a play on the name. Early a suffragan of Hierapolis, it counts eight bishops before 536.

The most celebrated is Theodoret, bishop from 423 to 458, a prolific writer known for his part in the Nestorian and Eutychian disputes. His small diocese, about forty miles square, held 800 churches, and a great basilica kept the relics of Saints Cosmas and Damian. Theodoret also wrote a whole work on the hermits of his territory, including Maron, patron of the Maronite Church. Justinian embellished and fortified the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cyzicus:
A historical entry describes Cyzicus, a titular see of Asia Minor and metropolis of the province of Hellespontus. Probably founded by Pelasgians from Thessaly and later colonized from Miletus, it rose after the Peloponnesian War as Athens and Miletus decayed. Alcibiades beat the Spartans there in 410 BC, Alexander took it from Persia in 334, and it withstood Mithridates' siege in 74 BC.

Rome favoured it and recognized its municipal freedom, and under Tiberius it became capital first of Mysia, then of Hellespontus, ranking among the world's greatest cities. Its coin, the Cyzicenus, was worth 28 drachmae. Arabs captured it in 675, earthquakes ruined it in 443 and 1043, and it was deserted by the eleventh century. Huge ruins still mark the site among the marshes of Balkiz Serai.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-damascus:
A city entry calls Damascus, in Syria, among the world's oldest cities, founded by Us, grandson of Shem, according to Josephus, and named in the Bible from Abraham's time. Under Solomon it became capital of an independent kingdom, warred often with Israel, and fell to Assyria's Tiglath-Pileser III in 734 BC after a two-year siege. Greek, Roman, and Arab rulers followed.

Sections trace the Greek city, the see of Damascus with its suffragans under Antioch, the Turkish city on the Barada river amid the gardens of the Ghouta, and modern religious conditions. Damascus is a Latin titular archbishopric and a metropolitan see for Melchite Greeks, Catholic Syrians, and Maronites, served by Jesuits, Franciscans, Sisters of Charity, and native Mariamet sisters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dardanus:
A short entry describes Dardanus, a titular see in Hellespont, suffragan to Cyzicus, with four or five bishops known from 431 or 451 to 879. The see appears in lists of bishoprics running into the twelfth or thirteenth century. The ancient town stood some seven miles south-west of the Dardanelles, near Kefez Bournou.

Its modern representative is the town called Dardanelles, an important port on the straits joining the Marmora to the Mediterranean, with about 8,000 people, Turks, Greeks, Jews, Armenians, and Europeans. A secular priest serves its small Catholic parish, and Georgian Sisters run its school, beside an American Protestant mission. Ships must stop to show the sultan's firman, and nearby Hissarlik holds Schliemann's famous excavations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daughters-of-:
A congregational entry describes the Daughters of Jesus, founded in 1834 at Kermaria in the Diocese of Vannes, France, to care for the sick poor and educate girls. Government authorization followed on 31 October 1842. Canada gained a provincial house at Three Rivers in 1893.

In Canada the sisters numbered 267 in 1910, choir and lay. They ran 25 schools, chiefly model and elementary, plus nine boarding schools, one hospital, and one orphanage. They also kept house for two religious communities. In the United States they ran a Lewiston, Montana, academy and hospital, and the school of the French parish at Waltham, Massachusetts. Worldwide the congregation counted over 200 convents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-scotus:
A biographical entry examines David Scotus, a medieval Irish chronicler dead in 1139. Early in the twelfth century a teacher named David lived at Wurzburg, and his surname Scotus suggests Irish origin, though he may be the Bishop of Bangor in Wales. Emperor Henry V, charmed by his virtue and learning, made him an imperial chaplain and took him to Italy in 1100 as royal historiographer.

His three-book history survives only in excerpts, above all in Ekkehard and William of Malmesbury, who notes its partiality for the king. A David consecrated Bishop of Bangor in April 1120 may be the same man, and as bishop he attended English synods and probably died in 1139. A later claim that he became a monk at Wurzburg's Saint James abbey clashes with that abbey's founding in 1140.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-decimus-magnu:
A biographical entry follows Decimus Magnus Ausonius, professor and poet born about AD 310 and dead about 394. Son of a Bordeaux physician, he studied at Bordeaux and Toulouse under his uncle Arborius. Returning to Bordeaux, he became professor of grammar, then of rhetoric. Between 364 and 368 Valentinian brought him to Trier as tutor to his son Gratian.

Ausonius joined the emperor's campaign against the Alemanni, receiving a young Swabian girl, Bissula, as booty. Honours followed: he governed Gaul as prefect, then the West with his son, and became consul in 379. After Gratian's murder in 383 he retired to Bordeaux among admiring friends and wrote much poetry. His short miscellaneous works include epigrams, eulogies of kin, a portrait of a fourth-century university, and the Mosella on the Moselle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-decius:
A biographical entry presents Decius, Roman Emperor from 249 to 251, born to a Roman or Romanized family near Sirmium in Pannonia. Almost nothing is known of his early career, spent largely in the army. He was the first great soldier-emperor from the Danube provinces, under whom senatorial rule ended and government became absolute monarchy.

Victory over Philip at Verona secured his throne, and he launched sweeping reforms of administration. Most of his reign passed at the head of legions repelling Gothic invaders from the Balkans, until defeat in the Dobrudscha marshes cost his life, his body never recovered. At home his impractical plan to reform morals by restoring old religion brought persecution of Christians and bitter schisms over the pardon of the lapsed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-delcus:
A short entry describes Delcus, a titular see of Thrace suffragan to Philippopolis. Its Greek name was Delkos or Delkoi, later Derkos, the form that prevailed, and its Turkish and common name is Derkos. Now a little village south-west of Kara Bournou on the Black Sea, it stands on Lake Derkos's southern bank, whose waters an aqueduct carries to Constantinople, with about 300 inhabitants.

Though some link its origin to Saint Andrew's preaching, the see is unmentioned before the eighth century, though Balsamon permits supposing it arose shortly after the Trullan Council of 692. Gregory, its first known bishop, attended Nicaea II in 787. Later prelates include Photius's partisan Neophytus and Ignatius's partisan Macarius, and John, who subscribed a synodal sentence in 997. In 1316 the see passed to Nymphaeum's deprived archbishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-demetrius:
A historical entry untangles four men named Demetrius in Scripture. Demetrius Soter, Saviour, reigned in Syria from 162 to 150 BC, having escaped Roman hostage years with Polybius's help to seize the Seleucid throne. Invited by foes of Judas Maccabeus, he sent Bacchides and Nicanor against the Maccabees, and Bacchides slew Judas at Berea.

Demetrius Nicator, Conqueror, succeeded in tangled Seleucid wars also touching Jewish history. The New Testament adds two more men of the name. Demetrius the silversmith of Acts chapter 19 stirred a riot at Ephesus to defend Artemis's shrine trade against Paul. Demetrius of Third John is praised for truth and good report, and may have borne the letter. The entry separates each figure's career with sources from Josephus, Justin, and Appian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denis-de-fray:
A life of Denis de Frayssinous, bishop and preacher, born in 1765 at Curières and dead in 1841. His conferences at Notre-Dame in Paris made him a leading voice in restoring French faith after the Revolution. Napoleon halted his preaching in 1809, yet he resumed in 1814 and carried on, with one short break, until 1822.

Napoleon still valued him, naming him a university councillor, and he later became grand master of the university and a member of the French Academy. As minister of public worship in 1824 he shielded the returning Fathers of the Faith, forerunners of the Jesuits. His public career ended with the revolution of 1830, and he spent his last years tutoring the Duke of Bordeaux and living at Saint-Geniez.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-desiderius-er:
A life of Desiderius Erasmus, called the most brilliant leader of German humanism, born at Rotterdam probably in 1466 and dead at Basle in 1536. The illegitimate son of Gerard of Gouda and Margaretha Rogers, he caught his love of humanism at Hegius's school in Deventer from age nine. Both parents died by his thirteenth year. Guardians sent him to Hertogenbosch for two lost years, and need forced him into the Emmaus monastery in 1486, a step he called his greatest misfortune.

Left free to study, he poured himself into the classics and rose to fame across Europe. The Praise of Folly, written in 1509, ran through seven editions in months, and his Greek New Testament of 1516 became the base of the received text. A brief Greek chair at Cambridge and a councillor's post under Archduke Charles frame his years. Long ties with the Basle printer Froben kept his books in print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-devotion-to-t:
A two-part entry on devotion to the Sacred Heart, first doctrinal, then historical. Its object is the Heart of flesh as symbol of the love of Jesus. A sensible element and a spiritual element join as one object, much as body and soul form one person, with love as the principal part. Foundations are weighed three ways, historical, theological, and scientific, and the proper act is love returned for love.

History runs from devotion to God's love in John and Paul toward the modern form, with Saint Margaret Mary's visions treated as spur rather than proof. Rome judged the worship on its own merits, and Pius the Sixth vindicated it in Auctorem fidei in 1794. Practices, associations, and a strong social character follow, with French Catholics named as clinging to it as a hope of ennoblement and salvation.
