catholic-encyclopedia-1913-olenus: Olenus was a city of ancient Achaia important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from ancient Greece.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-olympus: Olympus was a city of ancient Lycia important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Anatolian coast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ombus: Ombus, or Ombos, was a city of ancient Egypt important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Nile valley.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orcistus: Orcistus was a city of ancient Phrygia important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Anatolian plateau.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oremus: Oremus, let us pray, is the invitation that opens the Church's great collects. This entry explains its use, its history, and its liturgical place. Two words that gather the Church: the Oremus opens every great collect of the Roman Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orientius: This biographical entry profiles Orientius, a bishop and Christian poet of 400s Gaul, tracing his career, his verses, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's patristic gallery, preserved among its records of Gallic poets.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orlando-de-la: Lassus was the most famous composer of the Renaissance after Palestrina, master of the Munich court. This entry covers his career, his masses and motets, and his fame. The prince of musicians: his 2,000 works filled the courts of Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oropus: Oropus was a city of ancient Boeotia important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from ancient Greece.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orsisius: This biographical entry profiles Orsisius, an abbot of the Egyptian desert in the 300s, tracing his career, his rule, and his place among the desert fathers as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's monastic gallery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ortwin-gratiu: Ortwin Gratius was the Cologne humanist mocked in the Letters of Obscure Men for defending scholasticism. This entry covers his career, his learning, and the famous satire. The scholar the humanists loved to hate: his learning outlasted all their mockery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ottmar-luscin: Ottmar Luscinius was the Strasbourg humanist whose music and satires delighted the German Renaissance. This entry covers his career, his works, and his place. The nightingale of humanism: his Latin name truly means nightingale when it is rendered in Greek.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oxyrynchus: Oxyrhynchus was the Egyptian city whose rubbish heaps yielded the greatest papyrus treasure ever found. This entry covers its bishops, its church, and its manuscripts. The city of the papyri: its countless fragments preserve lost gospels and long-vanished ancient plays.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pacandus: Pacandus was a city of the ancient world important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the ancient map.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pacificus: This biographical entry profiles Pacificus, a Franciscan of the early order, tracing his career, his place among St. Francis's companions, and his memory as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Franciscan gallery, preserved among the first companions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palladius: This biographical entry profiles Palladius, a churchman of the early centuries, tracing his career, his writings, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's patristic gallery, preserved among the records of the early bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paltus: Paltus was a city of ancient Syria important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Levantine coast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pamelius: Pamelius was the Bruges bishop whose editions of Tertullian and Cyprian gave the Counter-Reformation its Fathers. This entry covers his career, his editions, and his scholarship. The editor of the African Fathers: his learned texts armed the Catholic controversialists well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-panemotichus: Panemotichus was a city of the ancient world important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the ancient map.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pantaenus: Pantaenus was the Sicilian bee who founded Christian philosophy at Alexandria, teaching Clement. This entry covers his career, his school, and his legacy. The first master of the catechetical school: his brilliant pupil Clement would one day far surpass him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paphnutius: St. Paphnutius was the one-eyed confessor-bishop whose sufferings shamed the Arians at Nicaea. This entry traces his confessorship, his role at the council, and his legend. The living martyr of the council: his terrible scars utterly silenced the Arian bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paralus: Paralus was a city of ancient Egypt important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Nile delta.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parnassus: Parnassus was both Apollo's mountain and a Christian bishopric of ancient Phocis. This entry notes its classical fame, its site, and its church history. The mountain of the Muses, made Christian: its bishops appear in the most ancient council lists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-the-deac: Paul the Deacon was the Lombard monk whose History of the Lombards is our chief source for his people. This entry covers his career, his history, and his scholarship. The Herodotus of the Lombards: his history preserved a vanished kingdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulus-barbus: This biographical entry profiles Paulus Barbus, a churchman of the early modern era, tracing his career and his service as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's gallery of prelates, preserved among its early modern churchmen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulus-jovius: Paolo Giovio was the Renaissance bishop whose histories and portrait museum made him famous across Europe. This entry covers his career, his works, and his museum on Lake Como. The historian of his age: his portraits preserved the faces of the mighty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulus-orosiu: Orosius was the Spanish priest whose Seven Books Against the Pagans answered the charge that Christianity ruined Rome. This entry covers his career, his history, and his influence. Augustine's historian: his universal chronicle taught the wondering Middle Ages its past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulus-venatu: This biographical entry profiles Paulus Venatus, a churchman of the early modern era, tracing his career and his service as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's gallery of prelates, preserved among its early modern churchmen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pednelissus: Pednelissus was a city of ancient Pisidia important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Anatolian highlands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-nunez-n: Pedro Nunes was the Portuguese mathematician whose loxodromes guided the age of discovery. This entry covers his career, his science, and his influence. The cosmographer of the caravels: his ingenious nonius greatly refined the navigator's difficult and dangerous art at sea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peregrinus: This biographical entry profiles Peregrinus, a Christian of the early Church, tracing his story and its significance as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's patristic gallery, preserved among its records of early Christian witnesses and martyrs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pergamus: Pergamus was the great city of Asia Minor where Satan's throne stood, in Revelation's words. This entry covers its bishops, its ruins, and its fame. The city of the martyred Antipas: its great library was called the wonder of antiquity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-person-gobeli: Gobelinus Persona was the Westphalian chronicler whose history preserves Paderborn's medieval story. This entry covers his career, his chronicle, and its value. The annalist of the Saxon Church: his vast Cosmidromius spans all creation right down to his own day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pessinus: Pessinus was a city of ancient Galatia important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Anatolian plateau.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-corneli: Peter Cornelius was the composer of The Barber of Bagdad, friend of Wagner and Liszt. This entry covers his career, his operas, and his songs. The poet-composer of the New German school: his lovely songs have long outlived his operas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-mongus: Peter Mongus was the Monophysite patriarch of Alexandria, intruded and deposed in turn. This entry explains his career, his heresy, and his stormy patriarchate. The stammerer on Peter's throne: his cruel nickname mocked his stammering speech unkindly at the court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-paludan: Peter Paludanus was the Dominican theologian whose commentaries shaped fourteenth-century thought. This entry covers his career, his works, and his influence. The patriarch-theologian of Jerusalem: his massive Sentences commentary long guided generations in the great Parisian schools of medieval theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-ramus: Peter Ramus was the French logician who defied Aristotle and died in the St. Bartholomew's massacre. This entry covers his logic, his career, and his death. The martyr of method: his bold new Dialectic once dethroned the ancient Aristotelian syllogism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petinessus: Petinessus was a city of ancient Galatia important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Anatolian plateau.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petrus-alphon: Petrus Alphonsus was the converted rabbi whose Disciplina Clericalis carried Eastern tales to the West. This entry covers his conversion, his works, and his influence. The storyteller of two worlds: his witty tales taught the wondering medieval West for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petrus-bernar: This biographical entry profiles Petrus Bernardinus, a churchman of the early modern era, tracing his career and his service as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's gallery of prelates, preserved among its early modern churchmen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petrus-de-nat: Petrus de Natalibus was the Venetian bishop whose Catalogus Sanctorum gathered the lives of the saints. This entry covers his career, his great collection, and its influence on hagiography. The bishop who catalogued heaven: his twelve books ordered the saints' year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petrus-diacon: Petrus Diaconus was the Montecassino monk whose chronicle preserves the abbey's medieval story. This entry covers his career, his writings, and their value to historians. The deacon-chronicler of the great abbey: his vivid pages span four troubled centuries of war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pez-bernhard-: The Pez brothers were the Benedictine scholars whose Thesaurus Anecdotorum rescued medieval manuscripts. This entry covers their careers, their editions, and their service to learning. The librarians of Melk abbey: their six great folio volumes preserved the medieval Middle Ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pharbaetus: Pharbaetus was a city of the Egyptian delta important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the ancient nomes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pharsalus: Pharsalus was the Thessalian plain where Caesar crushed Pompey in 48 BC, and its bishopric survives as a titular see. This entry covers its history, its bishops, and its fame. The field that decided Rome's fate: its dust buried the Republic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philoxenus: Philoxenus was the Monophysite bishop of Hierapolis whose Syriac version served his party. This entry explains his career, his heresy, and his Bible. The translator of the schism: his Syriac version served the Monophysite churches of Syria for long ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-photinus: Photinus was the bishop of Sirmium whose denial of Christ's divinity brought repeated condemnations. This entry explains his doctrine, his trials, and his stubborn persistence. The heretic of the Danube: his repeated depositions failed to silence his defiant public preaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-physiologus: The Physiologus was the ancient bestiary whose animal fables taught Christian morals. This entry traces its origins, its allegories, and its medieval popularity. The book of beasts that preached: its noble pelican taught Christ's selfless sacrifice on the Cross to all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierius: Pierius was the Alexandrian theologian called the younger Origen for his learning. This entry covers his career, his writings, and his influence. The Origen of the fourth century: his famed school rivaled great Alexandria's ancient catechetical fame itself in learning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pious-workers: The Pious Workers of St. Joseph Calasanctius are the religious devoted to Christian education. This entry covers their foundation, their rule, and their schools. The teachers of the poor after Calasanctius: their humble schools follow the great Pious Schools of Calasanz.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pityus: Pityus was a city of the ancient Black Sea coast important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Euxine shore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polybotus: Polybotus was a city of ancient Phrygia important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Anatolian plateau.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polycarpus: This biographical entry profiles Polycarpus, tracing his story and its significance as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's gallery of early Christians, preserved among its most ancient witnesses, martyrs, and holy saints of God forever.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pomponius-lae: Pomponius Laetus was the Roman humanist whose academy revived antiquity under the popes. This entry covers his career, his school, and his trial. The high priest of the Roman Renaissance: his bold academy defied the suspicious Paul II himself in Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontus: Pontus was the Black Sea kingdom of Mithridates, later a Roman province with Christian bishops. This entry covers its history, its sees, and its place in sacred geography. The land of the Amazons' legend: its ancient bishops sat at Nicaea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poor-brothers: The Poor Brothers of St. Francis are the religious devoted to teaching poor boys. This entry covers their foundation, their rule, and their schools. The brothers of the classroom poor: their simple vows bind them forever to the schools of the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-corneliu: Cornelius was the pope who faced the Novatian schism with Cyprian's help. This entry traces his pontificate, his mercy, and his martyrdom. The pope of the lapsed: his large mercy welcomed the weeping penitents home to peace and holy grace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-donus: Donus was the pope of 676 whose brief reign adorned Rome's churches. This entry notes his pontificate and the scant records as the 1913 editors found them. A quiet name of the seventh century: his pious works adorned the churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-formosus: Formosus was the pope whose corpse was tried in the Cadaver Synod. This entry traces his pontificate, his trial, and his vindication. The pope judged after death: his rotting corpse sat enthroned in the ghastly synod of 897 in judgment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-liberius: Liberius was the pope exiled for the Nicene faith under Constantius. This entry traces his pontificate, his banishment, and his vindication. The confessor of the Arian storm: his Beroean exile lasted two weary years in distant Thrace's winter cold and snow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-romanus: Romanus was the pope of 897 whose four months ended in deposition. This entry notes his brief pontificate and the scant records. A shadow of the Cadaver Synod's year: his sudden fall left no record behind him at all in history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-sabinian: Sabinianus was the pope who succeeded Gregory the Great in 604. This entry notes his brief pontificate and the legends of his avarice. The unpopular heir of the great Gregory: his miserly grain dole failed the hungry Romans in famine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-eu: Eutychianus was the saintly pope of the late 200s, martyr under Diocletian's shadow. This entry notes his pontificate and his veneration. A saint of the persecuted Church: his holy tomb draws the faithful still today in Christian Rome's dark catacombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-hi: Hilarus was the saintly pope who defended Chalcedon after Leo. This entry traces his pontificate, his decrees, and his sanctity. The guardian of the council's faith: his firm decrees ruled the Latin West alone in pure and holy orthodoxy forever.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-sy: Symmachus was the pope of the Laurentian schism's long war. This entry traces his pontificate, his rival, and his vindication. The victor of the double election: his Roman synods vindicated him at very long last indeed in holy Rome's councils.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-severinu: Severinus was the pope-elect who waited eighteen months for imperial confirmation. This entry notes his election, his delay, and his brief reign. The pope of the long vacancy: his saintly patience outlasted the stubborn Eastern emperor Heraclius himself in 640.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-sisinniu: Sisinnius was the pope whose reign lasted twenty days in 708. This entry notes his election, his gout, and his swift death. The pope of three weeks: his cruel gout crippled his brief reign entirely in constant pain and weakness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-adeod: Adeodatus was the saintly pope of the late 600s, gentle amid the plagues. This entry notes his pontificate, his charity, and his sanctity. The kindly pope of the pestilence: his holy prayers stayed the deadly Roman plague of 676's summer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-anacl: Anacletus was the saintly pope of the first century, Peter's near successor. This entry notes his pontificate, his martyrdom, and his veneration. A saint of the Church's infancy: his humble tomb lies in the Vatican hill today in eternal peace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-anice: Anicetus was the saintly pope who welcomed Polycarp to Rome. This entry traces his pontificate, the Easter dispute, and his martyrdom. The pope of the Quartodeciman debate: his large charity embraced old Polycarp in Rome itself with true Christian love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-anter: Anterus was the saintly pope martyred after forty days in 236. This entry notes his brief pontificate, his martyrdom, and his veneration. The pope of a single winter: his young blood bought the martyr's crown in 236's cold winter of persecution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-cletu: Cletus was the saintly pope of the first century, martyr under Domitian's shadow. This entry notes his pontificate and his veneration as the 1913 editors found them. A saint of the Church's dawn: his holy name endures in the Canon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-diony: Dionysius was the saintly pope of the late 200s who reorganized the parishes. This entry notes his pontificate, his reforms, and his veneration. The organizer of the persecuted Church: his ordered parishes survived Diocletian's fury intact and whole in faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-eleut: Eleutherius was the saintly pope of the legend of Lucius of Britain. This entry traces his pontificate, the British mission tale, and his sanctity. The pope of the first British Christians: his brave missionaries sailed north to Britain's distant shores.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-euseb: Eusebius was the saintly pope exiled to Sicily after two months in 310. This entry notes his brief pontificate, his banishment, and his veneration. The exile of the Constantinian dawn: his unjust banishment freed the suffering Church at long last.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-evari: Evaristus was the saintly pope of the early 100s, martyr in the apostolic age's wake. This entry notes his pontificate and his veneration as the 1913 editors found them. A saint of the second generation: his ordinations ordered the clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-hygin: Hyginus was the saintly pope of the mid-100s who ordered the Church's ranks. This entry notes his pontificate, his decrees, and his veneration. A saint of the apostolic age's evening: his wise decrees ordered the young Roman clergy in ranks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-linus: Linus was the second pope, Peter's immediate successor. This entry traces his pontificate, his martyrdom, and his veneration. The first heir of the fisherman: his holy name stands in the Roman Canon today and forevermore in every single daily prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-marce: Marcellinus was the saintly pope of Diocletian's great persecution. This entry traces his pontificate, the legends of his lapse, and his martyrdom. The pope of the bloodiest persecution: his heroic courage steadied the trembling Church of Rome itself in 304.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-silve: Silverius was the saintly pope starved by Belisarius's empress. This entry traces his pontificate, his deposition, and his martyrdom. The martyr of Theodora's wrath: his barren island became his lonely tomb in cruel exile in 538's bright June days of hunger.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-simpl: Simplicius was the saintly pope who watched the Western empire fall. This entry traces his pontificate, his firmness, and his sanctity. The pope of Rome's darkest hour: his steadfast faith outlasted the fallen empire of Rome itself in 476's autumn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-siric: Siricius was the saintly pope of the first papal decretals. This entry traces his pontificate, his letters, and his sanctity. The father of canon law's letters: his famous decretals ruled the whole Western Church in law and in holy love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-teles: Telesphorus was the saintly pope of the mid-100s, martyr under Hadrian's shadow. This entry notes his pontificate and his veneration as the 1913 editors found them. A saint of the apostolic age's evening: his midnight Christmas Mass endures to this day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-zephy: Zephyrinus was the saintly pope of the early 200s who fought the modalists. This entry notes his pontificate, his orthodoxy, and his veneration. The guardian against the Patripassians: his simple orthodoxy held the line in Rome itself for decades unbroken.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-zosim: Zosimus was the saintly pope of the Pelagian controversy's heat. This entry traces his pontificate, his vacillation, and his final firmness. The pope of the Tractoria: his final letters condemned Pelagius outright and wholly in 418's bright spring of grace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-vigilius: Vigilius was the pope dragged to Constantinople over the Three Chapters. This entry traces his pontificate, his vacillations, and his captivity. The pope of Justinian's council: his fearful vacillations shamed the apostolic see of Rome itself in 553's long council.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-praelatus-nul: A praelatus nullius is the prelate ruling a territory outside any diocese. This entry explains his jurisdiction, his rank, and the canon law. The abbot-bishop of the mission lands: his lone crozier rules the wild mission territory all alone in Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-primicerius: The primicerius was the first among the notaries and singers. This entry explains the office, its ranks, and its history. The chief of the papal choir: his ancient office crowned the papal singers of olden days in papal Rome itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priscianus: Priscianus was the great Latin grammarian of Constantinople. This entry notes his works, his influence, and his place in the schools. The grammarian of the late empire: his great Institutiones taught the medieval schools for centuries unchallenged in Latin grammar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-proconnesus: Proconnesus, the marble island of the Sea of Marmara, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its quarries and its early church history. A pale name from the Propontis: its white marble built the ancient churches of Byzantium.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prudentius: Prudentius was the Christian poet of late Roman Spain. This entry notes his hymns, his Psychomachia, and his fame. The Horace of the Christians: his burning hymns sang the Spanish martyrs of olden days gone by in song and verse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-publius-lentu: Publius Lentulus was the supposed author of the letter describing Christ. This entry examines the forgery, its text, and its vogue. The famous portrait that never was: its imagined lines shaped the sacred art of Christ for long centuries of faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quadratus: Quadratus was the earliest Christian apologist to the emperor. This entry notes his apology, his fragments, and his fame. The defender before Hadrian: his bold apology pleased the traveling emperor Hadrian himself in ancient Athens' marble courts of Roman law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raphael-badiu: Raphael Badius was the Dominican scholar and writer. This entry notes his career, his works, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A quiet name of the Preachers: his learned works fill the Dominican libraries of Italy's convents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ratramnus: Ratramnus was the Corbie monk of the Eucharistic controversy. This entry notes his treatise, his doctrine, and his influence. The theologian of the ninth century: his daring book troubled the medieval schools for centuries of fierce debate in Paris and beyond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rector-potens: Rector potens, verax Deus is the Tuesday hymn of Terce. This entry explains its author, its text, and its music. The hymn of the midday God: its stately verses praise the mighty Ruler of the noon hour in song and psalm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-com: The Religious Communities of the Name of Jesus are the sisterhoods under Christ's title. This entry notes their foundations, their works, and their spirit. The daughters of the Holy Name: their humble schools teach the children of France's towns and villages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhizus: Rhizus, the Pontic port of the Black Sea's eastern shore, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from Lazica: its dark waves beat the rocky shore of Pontus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhosus: Rhosus, the Cilician port of the Issic gulf, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from Cilicia: its ancient port faced the open sea of Cilicia's coast in the east.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ricardus-angl: Ricardus Anglicus was the English physician of the schools. This entry notes his medicine, his writings, and his age. The doctor of the thirteenth century: his learned books taught the medical schools of Paris and Montpellier in the 1200s' halls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-pullus: Robert Pullus, the theologian of the Paris schools, is treated under the variant of his name. This brief entry notes his writings and refers the reader to the fuller account. A scholastic of the twelfth century: his name doubles the cardinal's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-romulus-augus: Romulus Augustulus was the last emperor of the West. This entry notes his deposition, his pension, and his age. The boy of the fallen empire: his forced abdication ended Rome in 476's September days of fall and ruin and night.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sagalassus: Sagalassus, the Pisidian city of the Taurus foothills, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from Pisidia: its vast ruins crown the mountain in Pisidia's heights in Turkey.

china-and-the-manchus:
Herbert A. Giles, Cambridge professor of Chinese and a former consul at Ningpo, told the story of Manchu China from its origins to its fall. Giles begins with the Nü-chên and Kitan nomads north of Korea, then follows the fall of the Ming dynasty and the Manchu conquest. Chapters march emperor by emperor: Shun Chih, K'ang Hsi, Ch'ien Lung, and on through the troubled nineteenth century.

Foreign wars, rebellions, and court weakness fill the later reigns, until the boy emperor Hsüan T'ung gives way to Sun Yat-sen and the republic. Giles writes brisk, opinionated history for general readers, with a pronunciation guide and a list of works consulted. The book captures what Edwardian Britain knew, and guessed, about China.
christopher-columbus:
Mildred Stapley Byne's Christopher Columbus, from the True Stories of Great Americans series, tells the discoverer's life for young readers. Lowell lines on the title page set the theme. Europe's wise men sneered that all knowable earth was known, until one man from Genoa refused, and sailed toward an unknown world.

Chapters follow Columbus from his youth and his season of waiting through Isabella's decision. They continue through the cry of land, the natives of the new land, and the return in the Nina. Later chapters cover the second and third voyages, the return in disgrace, public sympathy, the last voyage, and the courage of Diego Mendez. Byne writes plainly and admiringly, making Columbus a hero of persistence for school readers.
coriolanus:
William Shakespeare's Coriolanus, his Roman tragedy of pride, appears in this old-spelling electronic text, prefaced by the same printer's notes used across this Shakespeare set. Caius Martius, named Coriolanus for his victory at Corioli, despises the Roman plebeians and their tribunes. The people, hungry for corn, despise him back.

Banished, he joins his enemy Aufidius and marches on Rome, where his mother Volumnia pleads him out of vengeance and into death. The middle scenes show the tribune Brutus charging that disdain mangles true judgment and robs the state of integrity. Shakespeare's coldest political play studies honor, class hatred, and a hero whose virtues fit war and ruin peace.
cratylus:
Plato's Cratylus, in Benjamin Jowett's translation, perplexed its own editor, who ranks it with Plato's best in fancy, humor, and style while doubting anyone has dispelled uncertainty about its aim. Hermogenes and Cratylus dispute whether names are correct by nature or by convention. Socrates, between them, improvises etymologies by the hundred.

Greek words are unfolded into hidden meanings, gods' names parsed, and letters assigned sounds and characters, until Socrates wonders whether language grew up largely independent of any name-giver. The dialogue founded the philosophy of language while mocking its own method. Jowett's introduction guides readers through the jest and the seriousness, which remain entangled by design.
dear-brutus:
J. M. Barrie's play Dear Brutus opens in a darkened room where its two chief characters, the stage directions say, are Darkness and Light. Outside lies Lob's moonlit garden, and Lob, an elfin old host, has gathered a house party of discontented guests. Each regrets some turning taken years before. Barrie builds the play on one wish: what if life offered a second chance?

In Act Two, the guests wander into a magic wood that appears for one midsummer night, and each lives the other life. The drunk becomes a great man, the childless woman gains a daughter, and the painter meets the family he never had. The wood grants wishes only to show that character travels with the traveler. Readers and audiences get Barrie's gentlest argument: people mostly become again what they already were, which makes the play's comedy tender rather than cruel.

euthydemus:
Plato's Euthydemus, in Benjamin Jowett's translation, is part comedy and part the oldest treatise on logic, as its introduction claims. Two sophist brothers, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, arrive in Athens boasting they can teach virtue and refute anything. Socrates asks them to demonstrate on the young Cleinias while his lover Ctesippus watches.

The brothers produce fallacies by the dozen: whatever is, cannot not be; fathers are dogs; learning is learning what you already know. Socrates, pretending earnestness, says he was the more decided because they seemed to jest. Beneath the clowning sits Plato's serious purpose, distinguishing real teaching from verbal victory. Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations later catalogued the very tricks laughed at here.
fables-for-the-frivolous:
Fables for the Frivolous, by Guy Wetmore Carryl and illustrated by Peter Newell, retells La Fontaine with apologies, as the subtitle says. Carryl's contents are a parade of paired adjectives. The Ambitious Fox meets the Unapproachable Grapes. The Persevering Tortoise faces the Pretentious Hare. Patrician Peacocks, an Arrogant Frog, and the Impecunious Cricket fill out the menagerie. The 1898 volume reprints pieces from Harper's periodicals, Life, and Munsey's Magazine.

Each fable is a short verse comedy with a moral turned sideways. Carryl was the American master of the form, a light versifier of real technical brilliance. His animals speak drawing room American. The morals land as jokes first and sermons never. Newell's illustrations match the wit line for line. The book remains the frivolous fable's high water mark in English: Aesop rewritten by a man who had been to the club and found it wanting.

Fame follows him into retreat, and temptation arrives as a beautiful visitor he escapes only by cutting off his own finger, which falls to the floor before the pain comes. Later failures humble him into anonymous wandering and service. Tolstoy wrote the story late, as a fierce examination of pride wearing the mask of holiness.
