govdocs-archive_org-oswald-spengler-hera: Oswald Spengler, the German historian known for The Decline of the West, wrote a study of Heraclitus, the early Greek thinker. Heraclitus taught that all things flow and change, and only fragments of his words survive. The edition includes a foreword by Rodolfo Mondolfo on how to interpret him. Spengler reads the fragments as one mind's whole view of the world, not as scattered sayings.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_afghanis:
As the Soviet war in Afghanistan wound down in the late 1980s, four powers circled the country's future. A New Phase in the Great Game follows the United States, the Soviets, India, and Pakistan as each tried to shape a new Afghanistan.

The Great Game was the old name for rivalry over Central Asia, and the briefing book argues it never really ended. Declassified records show diplomats and intelligence services backing clients and blocking rivals while Afghans bore the cost. The collection serves readers who want the end of the Soviet war told from the files of all four capitals.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_china_Ch: China's Tibet Problem: The Contentious History - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
In the 1950s the Soviet missile program was a hard target for American intelligence, meaning a secret very hard to penetrate. James E. David edited this briefing book, number 695, published in February 2020. It covers United States efforts against that program through 1957.

The failures are candid. Washington learned of the first Soviet ICBM test from a Soviet press release. News of the second came from a remark made to a French politician. Sputnik's launch caught the United States unaware until the satellite was in orbit. The record shows an intelligence system learning, expensively and in public, how much it did not know.

For sixty-five years the United States has tracked objects in orbit, building a space surveillance network to watch an ever more crowded sky. James E. David and Charles Byvik edited this briefing book, number 824, published in March 2023. Its title asks the network's three basic questions.

What is up there, where is it, and what is it doing: that is the daily work of cataloging satellites and debris. The documents span the effort from the early space age to today's congestion. Readers get the unglamorous backbone of space power, the tracking that makes both military planning and collision warnings possible.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: Castle BRAVO, detonated at Bikini Atoll in 1954, yielded far more power than its designers predicted and spread fallout over inhabited islands and a Japanese fishing boat. This briefing-book page marks seventy years since that shot, which its title calls the worst nuclear test in United States history. The evidence supplied here is the title alone, and the test documents are not described. BRAVO's legacy includes sick Marshall Islanders, a dead fisherman, and the modern politics of nuclear testing compensation.

Twice in 1979 and 1980, American warning systems reported Soviet missile attacks that were not happening, and United States forces went on alert. This briefing-book page presents the record of those false warnings. A companion Archive volume on Colonel Odom's four a.m. phone call covers the same alert system in detail. The evidence here is the title alone. The episodes remain the standard cautionary case in nuclear safety: minutes of confusion, inside a system built to react in minutes.

The United States Air Force filmed its own preparations for nuclear war, and some of that film has been declassified. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in March 2023, built around those movies. One shows the crew of an American bomber at work.

Evidence here is short, so description stays plain. Films made for training and morale show nuclear war as a job: checklists, uniforms, calm voices. That ordinariness is the historical point. Moving images of crews rehearsing the end of the world reveal how completely the mission had been normalized inside the service that would fly it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_southern:
Argentine generals seized power on March 24, 1976, opening seven years of military rule and mass repression. Briefing Book number 752, edited by Carlos Osorio and published in March 2021, asks a narrower question: what did the United States know before the coup, and when did it know it?

The documents show American officials had ample warning that a coup was being plotted, and kept a channel open to the plotters themselves. The Ford administration knew the military planned grave abuses against human rights. One episode stands out: the American ambassador stopped a pre-coup visit by a former deputy director of the CIA. For readers, the papers shift blame from surprise to choice, showing a government informed early and engaged anyway.
grass-of-parnassus:
Andrew Lang called his 1888 verses Grass of Parnassus, rhymes old and new, a modest title for polished occasional poetry. The contents sort poems as Deeds of Men, Rhodocleia, and Hesperothen, that last group returning to Homer's Phaeacia and the Sirens. Seekers for a city, the White Pacha, and Colonel Burnaby open the heroic section.

Lang writes of Burnaby and the Gordon relief expedition, twilight on Tweed, Clevedon church, and a strange rose that blossoms only in fairy tales heard at a nurse's knee. History, classics, and border scenery blend in his light forms: ballades, rondels, and songs. The volume shows the scholar-poet Lang between his translations of Homer and his fairy books.
greek-romances-heliodorus-longus-achille:
Rowland Smith translated three surviving Greek novels of love and adventure in one volume. Heliodorus wrote the Ethiopics, Longus wrote Daphnis and Chloe, and Achilles Tatius wrote Clitopho and Leucippe. All three date from the Roman imperial centuries.

Lovers are separated by pirates, storms, false deaths, and jealous rivals. Heliodorus opens in mid-action and unwinds his plot backward with great skill. Longus tells a gentler tale of two foundlings growing into love on Lesbos. Achilles Tatius favors lush description and narrow escapes. Together these romances show the ancient novel learning to entertain at length.
holberg-comedies-by-holberg-jeppe-of-the:
Ludvig Holberg, often called the Danish Moliere, wrote the three comedies gathered here in English. Jeppe of the Hill wakes a drunken peasant as a lord for a day. The Political Tinker mocks a craftsman who thinks he can run the state. Erasmus Montanus skewers a student drunk on Latin learning.

Each play turns one human folly into laughter with a kind edge. Peasants, burghers, and scholars all get their turn under Holberg's whip. The jokes still land because pride and pretence have not changed. These plays founded a stage tradition in Scandinavia and remain its comic bedrock.
josephus:
Josephus is Norman Bentwich's study of the ancient Jewish historian, published at Philadelphia in 1914. Bentwich had already written on Philo-Judaeus of Alexandria. Nine chapters run from The Jews and the Romans to a conclusion. A bibliography, a list of abbreviations, and an index support the text.

Two chapters follow Josephus's life to the fall of Jotapata and after his surrender to Rome. Others treat his works, his relation to earlier writers, and the Jewish Wars. Bentwich also sets Josephus beside the Bible and later Jewish history. A final chapter reads his apology as a defense of Judaism. The book introduces a writer whose histories remain a chief source for his age.
lives-of-girls-who-became-famous:
Sarah Knowles Bolton wrote these lives for aspiring girls in 1914. She had earlier written Poor Boys Who Became Famous. Her preface insists life is earnest activity, not a play-day. Goethe and Jean Ingelow supply mottoes about energy and work.

Bolton offers George Eliot and Rosa Bonheur as grand examples. Elizabeth Fry visited the poor and the prisoner instead. Mrs. Stowe and Miss Alcott lightened their parents' burdens by writing. Rich readers, like Baroness Burdett-Coutts, must bless the world generously. Mary Lyon's persistency shows poor girls what purpose can accomplish. Work is heaven's hest, Jean Ingelow's quoted line declares.
maitre-cornelius:
Maitre Cornelius is a tale by Honoré de Balzac, in Katharine Wormeley's translation. It opens on All Saints' Day, 1479, in the cathedral of Tours. Vespers are ending, and darkness fills the unfinished towers. Archbishop Hélie de Bourdeilles rises to bless the faithful.

In that candlelit gloom Balzac sets his medieval mystery. Cornelius is the aged treasurer and moneylender of King Louis XI. His hoarded gold and secret house draw young lovers into danger. A young nobleman risks all to reach the girl he loves. Balzac blends history, romance, and his great theme of money. The tale is the Human Comedy's medieval chapter.
mediaeval-lore-from-bartholomew-anglicus:
Robert Steele gathered Mediaeval Lore from Bartholomew Anglicus, with a preface by William Morris. Bartholomew was an English friar of the 1200s who wrote a vast store book. Steele picks its most curious entries for modern readers.

Morris opens by fighting the old view of the middle ages. That age, he says, was no mere chaos between two bright eras. He credits new study of history and art for the change. The lore itself ranges over beasts, plants, stones, and the skies. A picture of thinkers on Mount Olympus fronts the book. Keats lines on holy air and water set its mood.
menexenus:
Menexenus is a short dialogue attributed to Plato, presented here in Benjamin Jowett's translation. In it, Socrates recites a funeral oration over Athens's war dead. He claims, with a straight face, that Aspasia taught it to him. The speech praises Athens in the grand style of public oratory.

Jowett's appendix, printed with the text, weighs doubts about which Platonic works are genuine. Funeral speeches, he notes, are exactly the kind of writing most open to forgery. He explains how unknown works easily gained a famous author's name. Read together, speech and appendix raise sharp questions about rhetoric, patriotism, and authorship.
moon-of-israel-a-tale-of-the-exodus:
H. Rider Haggard set this tale of the Exodus in ancient Egypt, narrated by the scribe Ana. His author's note argues a bold thesis about Pharaoh. The real Pharaoh of the Exodus, he suggests, was the usurper Amenmeses. Amenmeses held the throne briefly between Meneptah and Seti II, and his body has never been found.

Chapters move from Tanis to the land of Goshen, with the breaking of a cup and a prophecy. Seti counsels Pharaoh, Amon is smitten, and the Nile runs red. Haggard meant to dedicate the book to Egyptologist Gaston Maspero, who died during the war. The note adds the dedication at his family's wish.
mucedorus:
Mucedorus is an old stage comedy of love and danger in two kingdoms. Its full title names Prince Mucedorus of Valencia and Amadine of Aragon. The cast lists kings, nobles, a maid, and councillors. Scenes move between courts and a wild forest.

The catalog credits the play to William Shakespeare, as old editions did. V1 notes it was acted by his company and loved in its day. A prince in disguise seeks the princess he loves. A wild man of the woods adds threat and fun. Scholars still debate who wrote it, which makes this popular romance a neat puzzle of the early stage.
nasa-tm-19650019798-rocket-motor-spin-te:
Robert L Swain, Melvin H Lucy, and Peter H Foss at Langley described a spin-test rig for solid rocket motors in October 1964. Some motors behave differently while spinning in flight. Burning and gas flow inside the motor can change under spin. Hot residue can also settle in new places, raising the risk of failure.

Their apparatus subjects a motor to spin or roll while it is tested on the ground. That lets engineers reproduce flight conditions safely. The paper was given at a static testing meeting in California. Ground spin tests offered a way to find spin-related faults before a motor ever flew.
nasa-tm-19700011382-sound-measurements-o:
Loren W. Acker, Joseph R. Balombin, and James W. Coats of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in March 1970. They measured the sound made by a high-bypass turbofan engine. The engine gave four thousand pounds of thrust in the tests.

Sound data were taken at several engine speeds. The team also varied the nozzle areas of the fan and the core engine. One strong single tone stood out above the rest of the noise, they found. It matched the rate at which the fan blades passed a fixed point. The report gives the noise levels that listeners would perceive at those settings.
nasa-tm-19720014944-precipitation-criter:
Glenn E Daniels of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote these precipitation guidelines on March 22, 1972, as NASA TM X-64650. Daniels worked in the Aero Astrodynamics Laboratory. Rockets and spacecraft must survive rain while waiting and launching. Designers need agreed extremes of rainfall to build against. This document supplies those numbers for NASA vehicle development. It pairs with his broader climate criteria work.

The guidelines give likely extremes and traits of precipitation. Rainfall rate chances form the core of the data. Drop size and the speed at which drops fall are included. Wind speeds that come with rain also matter for loads on a waiting vehicle. Associated equipment falls under the same guidance. Weather criteria like these quietly shape launch site rules.
nautilus:
Laura E. Richards published Nautilus in Boston in 1895, and this copy marks the tenth thousand printed. Estes and Lauriat issued it, with pictures. Richards had already written Captain January and Melody. She dedicated the story to the Howe Club of Gardiner, Maine.

Early chapters meet the boy John, then a skipper, then a great exhibition. John goes aboard the Nautilus, and a chapter named Mystery follows. The chapter heads alone promise a sea tale for young readers, built around a boy and a ship. Richards writes with warmth, and the sea setting gives the story its pull.
old-scores-and-new-readings-discussions-:
John Runciman wrote these essays on music and musicians. The book appeared in London in the year 1901. The contents begin with William Byrd and his Mass. Henry Purcell is called our last great musician. Bach, Handel, Haydn, and Mozart receive long essays.

Later pieces treat Schubert, Weber, Wagner, and Verdi. Famous operas such as Tristan and Lohengrin are discussed. Runciman gives firm, personal judgments on each composer. He asks readers to hear old scores with fresh ears. The book suits music lovers who enjoy strong opinions. Its essays span four centuries of European music.
peck-s-bad-boy-with-the-circus: The sample hosted for this entry shows only the front matter of Peck's Bad Boy with the Circus, the title pages and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names George W. Peck and promises the experiences of the Bad Boy and his dad travelling with a circus, the boy getting his father into hot water with everyone from the clown to the elephant. The contents begin with the Bad Boy keeping a diary and his dad becoming a circus manager.
phaedrus:
Plato's Phaedrus, in Benjamin Jowett's translation, joins the Symposium as Plato's great work on love. Jowett's introduction says the dialogue may be about love, or rhetoric, or the union of the two. Its scene is a walk outside Athens, where Phaedrus carries a speech by the rhetorician Lysias hidden under his cloak.

Socrates lures him to a plane tree by the Ilissus stream, where they read the speech and answer it. Socrates refuses to waste time explaining away myths like Boreas and Oreithyia; the proper study of mankind is man. From that shade come the myth of the soul's chariot and a lasting critique of writing.
philebus:
Plato's Philebus, in Benjamin Jowett's translation, asks whether pleasure or wisdom makes the better life. Jowett's introduction calls it one of Plato's later writings, where the speculative element has grown and the dramatic has thinned. Great advances in abstract thought, he says, come with a laboured march and some confusion in the design.

Socrates argues against Philebus and Protarchus for a mixed life measured by reason. Jowett honestly lists the dialogue's unreconciled points, including its table of goods. Readers who persist get Plato's deepest treatment of pleasure, pain, limit, and the good.
poems-patriotic-religious-miscellaneous:
Father Abram J. Ryan, the Catholic priest who became known as the poet laureate of the Confederacy, wrote the poems sorted here under three heads: patriotic, religious, and miscellaneous. Ryan served as a chaplain in the Confederate army and afterward in parishes across the South, and his verse mourned the lost cause while preaching his faith. His most famous piece, the Conquered Banner, taught a defeated people to furl their flag with reverence.

The patriotic poems carry that mourning: flags, graves, and the honor of the dead. Religious poems turn from country to church, in the voice of a priest who wrote hymns and meditations for his flock. Miscellaneous pieces fill out the man, occasional, personal, and lyrical. Ryan's fame has faded outside the South, yet for generations of southern readers his was the voice that put their grief into meter, and this three-part collection is his monument.
polly-of-the-circus:
Margaret Mayo wrote Polly of the Circus, first a hit play and then a novel, dedicating it to her little mother in German endearment. The opening scene sits the reader inside the women's dressing tent of the Great American Circus while the band plays noisily outside: trunks belching satins and paste jewels. Tights drying on ropes, performers making up by lamplight, and one wistful girl on a camp chair seeing none of it, long hardened to the glitter.

Polly is a bareback rider whose world is sawdust, and the story carries her out of it. Into the quiet household of a young minister after an accident, where circus and parsonage judge each other and both change. Mayo's tale was a sensation of its era, filmed and refilmed. The dressing-tent chapter alone, observed like a painting, explains why audiences believed in Polly completely.
prince-fortunatus:
William Black published Prince Fortunatus with Harper and Brothers in New York in 1905, in an illustrated edition. Black, author of A Princess of Thule, was the Victorian novelist of the Scottish Highlands, and his hero here divides his life between the two worlds of the contents. A rehearsal, the great god Pan, and Nina open a theatrical story in London, while Strathaivron. The twelfth of August, the phantom stag, and Highland place names carry the second half to the deer forests.

The prince of the title is an actor, whose stage triumphs and country-house sporting life Black braids into one career of charm. An illustration at the front shows a woman dragging off her engagement ring and dashing it at a man's feet, the melodrama promised early and delivered late. Black's scenic storytelling made him a bestseller; this novel is his manner complete.
quaint-gleanings-from-ancient-poetry-a-c:
Quaint Gleanings from Ancient Poetry gathers curious poems of the sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth centuries, edited from manuscripts and rare printed books by Edmund Goldsmid. His introduction, written at Edinburgh on March 6, 1884, presents the book as volume one of the Collectanea Adamantaea.

Goldsmid collected the pieces over years of reading in odd corners: library manuscripts, books from dusty stalls and auction rooms, even pencil notes inside torn bindings. The contents mix song, grave and gay. One poem is Anthony Munday's, on the captivity of John Fox. A letter from the Duke of Monmouth appears. A satire against the Scots is included. A dirge is singled out for praise.
quiet-talks-about-jesus: Quiet Talks about Jesus, by S. D. Gordon, author of Quiet Talks on Power and Quiet Talks on Prayer, is shown here by its contents alone. Three parts treat the purpose of Jesus. They treat the person of Jesus, human and divine. They treat the great experiences of his life too. Those are the Jordan, the wilderness, and the transfiguration. Gethsemane, Calvary, the resurrection, and the ascension complete the list. Study notes close the book, under sayings of Moses and Paul about glory.
quotes-and-images-from-christopher-colum:
Quotes and Images from Columbus takes its extracts from Christopher Columbus, Filson Young's life of the explorer, and sets them in alphabetical order as short, sharp lines. Young, we are told at the head, called his book Columbus by Young, and the extracts keep his critical tone.

Columbus stands accused in these lines of a habit of untruthfulness about his own past and of offering bargains to the Almighty. Other entries touch the egg wager. They touch Amerigo Vespucci. They touch the claim that the Spaniards came from heaven. Cannibal tastes appear too. So does the old fight over the roundness of the earth. That roundness was denied, Young notes, even in the Christian era.
roget-s-thesaurus: Peter Mark Roget's thesaurus of English words and phrases stands behind this electronic version. A long note at the front explains that the text derives from the edition of 1911, prepared by MICRA, Inc., which makes no claim on the version. More than a thousand words absent from the printed book have been added, the note says. Many modern words are still missing, and some fifteen hundred common verbs cannot be found here. Old and foreign words are marked in square brackets. No page of the word lists themselves is shown.
salads-sandwiches-and-chafing-dish-daint: Janet McKenzie Hill wrote Salads, Sandwiches and Chafing-Dish Dainties, with fifty illustrations of original dishes, in a new edition with additional recipes issued at Boston in 1909. Hill is named as editor of The Boston Cooking-School Magazine and author of Practical Cooking and Serving. Copyrights of 1899 and 1903 stand on the title page. A front picture shows a table laid for Sunday-night tea. Hill gives the book to Mrs. William B. Sewall, president of the Boston Cooking-School Corporation.
septimus: William J. Locke wrote this novel, first copyright in 1908 and issued by Dodd, Mead and Company in New York. The pages at hand show a list of Locke's many other books, among them Simon the Jester and The Beloved Vagabond, plus the title page of a 1931 printing. No contents list, chapter text, or cast of persons appears in these opening pages. Who Septimus is, and what befalls him, cannot be stated fairly from the title pages alone.
songs-of-angus-and-more-songs-of-angus: Violet Jacob, author of Flemington, wrote Songs of Angus, first published in 1915 and printed in this John Murray issue at London in 1919. Two small books of her poems are joined in one text. Jacob thanks the editors of the Cornhill Magazine, Country Life, and The Outlook for leave to reprint pieces they had printed. The contents name Tam i' the Kirk, The Howe o' the Mearns, The Lang Road, and The Beadle o' Drumlee.
stories-that-words-tell-us:
Elizabeth O'Neill wrote Stories That Words Tell Us, printed at London in 1918. O'Neill, also the author of The World's Story and A Nursery History of England, turns here from events to language itself, treating common words as small storehouses of the past.

Her contents begin with British history told from English words, then how we got our Christian names and surnames, and the stories hidden in place names. Later parts cover new names for new places, old London names, words made by great writers, words the Bible gave us, and words taken from the names of people, animals, and places. It is history taught through the words children use every day.
tanakh-jps-1917-exodus:
Exodus, second book of the Torah, is given in the Jewish Publication Society's English rendering of 1917, made from the Masoretic Text. The book opens by naming the sons of Israel who came down into Egypt with Jacob, seventy souls in all.

Joseph and his brothers die, yet their kin grow strong and fill the land. A new king who never knew Joseph fears their numbers and sets taskmasters over them. Forced to build the store towns Pithom and Raamses, they still grow more. Readers stand at the start of slavery in Egypt, the hard ground from which cries for freedom, plagues, and a sea crossing will soon rise.
tanakh-jps-1917-leviticus:
Leviticus, third book of the Torah, appears in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 English rendering of the Holy Scriptures. God calls Moses from the tent of meeting and gives him rules to pass to the children of Israel.

First come the laws of gifts brought to the altar, starting with the burnt gift taken from herd or flock. A male beast without flaw is brought to the tent door, and the giver lays a hand on its head. Priests, the sons of Aaron, dash the blood and lay the parts in order on the fire. Readers get a dense code of worship, purity, feasts, and right living at the heart of the Torah.
ted-strong-s-motor-car-or-fast-and-furio:
Edward C. Taylor wrote Ted Strong's Motor Car, or Fast and Furious, in 1915 for his Ted Strong tales of the Moon Valley Ranch. Ted leads the broncho boys, a band of young ranch hands led in fun and work by his cool head.

Chapter one, Talking About Smart Hogs, opens with a row in the ranch living room over a trained pig. Carl Schwartz swears he will kill the hog, while Bud Morgan claims he owns its best part, the head, and taught it tricks. Carl vows to cut its tail to spoil the act. Readers get slangy ranch fun, fast cars, and boy-hero deeds in a dime-novel key.
thaumaturgia-or-elucidations-of-the-marv: Thaumaturgia, or Elucidations of the Marvellous, is by an Oxonian. It came out in 1835. A verse from Hudibras stands at its front. It tells of Bombastes and the devil's bird in his sword pommel. Chapters listed cover the study of demons first. They take up the devil's bent for old women. Magic and its rites come next, with Jewish magi. Kinds of magic then follow. They include augury from the flight and feeding of birds. Omens drawn from sacrifice are also named.
the-1990-united-states-census:
The 1990 United States Census, as set out here, sorts the states into four regions and gives head counts for the nation, each region, and each state. The Northeast holds nine states, the South sixteen, the Midwest twelve, and the West thirteen.

A table dated to a November 7, 1991 release puts the United States total at 248,709,873 people. The Northeast counts 50,809,229 and the Midwest 59,668,632, while a later estimate dated December 29, 1994 lifts the national count to 261,653,497. Readers get the raw shape of the 1990 count, useful for tracing where Americans lived at the start of the decade.
the-adventures-of-a-special-corresponden:
Jules Verne wrote The Adventures of a Special Correspondent Among the Various Races and Countries of Central Asia, the tale of Claudius Bombarnac of the Twentieth Century paper. A life and book list at the front notes Verne's birth at Nantes in 1828 and death in 1905.

That note lists his famed books with dates, from A Voyage to the Center of the Earth in 1864 to The Brothers Kip in 1902. Chapter one then finds Bombarnac at Tiflis in Transcaucasia on May 13, reading a wire that names him as special correspondent there. Readers ride with him on the great Trans-Asian railway toward Peking, through a comic mix of peoples, plots, and a secret cargo.
the-age-of-big-business-a-chronicle-of-t:
Burton J. Hendrick wrote The Age of Big Business, a chronicle of the captains of industry, printed at New Haven by Yale University Press in 1919. Seven chapters run from industrial America at the Civil War's end through the first great trust, steel, the telephone, and the car made common.

Hendrick begins by picturing the country as the war closed. It would look strange to modern eyes, he argues. Most plain means of comfort that now vex men with cost and rule had yet to appear. Readers then trace how trusts, steel mills, wires, light and power firms, farm machines, and cheap cars built a new corporate America in two generations.
the-anti-slavery-examiner-omnibus: A gathered set of tracts from the American Anti-Slavery Society, dated 1836, is listed here under the head The Anti-Slavery Examiner. Number one addresses the people of the United States who value their rights. Number two appeals to the Christian women of the South, in both first and revised forms. Gerrit Smith writes to the Reverend James Smylie of Mississippi in number three. Number four argues the Bible against slavery more than once, and number five takes up Congress's power over the District of Columbia.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-2-exod:
Exodus in King James wording, begins by naming the children of Israel who came into Egypt, each man with his household, with Jacob. Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Benjamin, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher are listed.

Seventy souls came from Jacob, with Joseph already in Egypt. Joseph dies, as does that whole generation, yet Israel multiplies until the land is filled. A new king who did not know Joseph tells his people that Israel is more and mightier than they are. He urges dealing wisely with them, lest they grow still stronger. Oppression follows fear.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-3-levi:
Leviticus in King James wording, begins with God calling Moses and speaking from the tabernacle of the congregation. Any man bringing an offering must bring it from the herd or the flock.

A burnt sacrifice from the herd must be a male without blemish, offered willingly at the tabernacle door. The offerer lays his hand on its head, so it may be accepted to make atonement for him. He kills the bullock before the Lord, and Aaron's sons bring the blood and sprinkle it around the altar. Flaying follows. Detailed ritual law, step by step, fills the opening.
the-boy-with-the-u-s-census: Francis Rolt-Wheeler wrote The Boy with the U.S. Census, dated November 1911, with thirty-eight plates drawn in the main from United States bureaus. Rolt-Wheeler gave the book to Hamilton Day. The chapters start with A Blood Feud in Old Kentucky. Rescuing a Lost Race and A Manufactory of Rifles come next. Then a boy leads a crusade, and a mother faces being sent away. Hoboes on the tramp and census heroes of the frozen north fill the mid heads.
the-certainty-of-a-future-life-in-mars-b:
Bradford Torrey Dodd left these posthumous papers, edited by L. P. Gratacap and published by Brentano's in 1903. Their claim is bold: a future life on Mars, reported as fact. Dodd died at Christ Church, New Zealand, in January 1895, after a long illness in which consumption set in.

The editor's preface explains how the manuscript reached him and why he trusts it. The illness, he reports, was blamed on exposure Dodd faced while receiving wireless messages tied to his strange history. Gratacap did not know Dodd, but inquiries since have convinced him the papers were no hoax. Dodd's skill in science was marked, and he and his father had worked at an astronomical station near Christ Church. Readers get the account on those terms: a sincere, odd claim from a man of science.
the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-part-: Miscellaneous pieces close the Artemus Ward series in part 7, by the record title's account. Charles Farrar Browne wrote them all under the Ward name. Only a Gutenberg header is present, though, donations appeal included.No pages of the work itself follow the front matter. It is the last of the seven parts in the Gutenberg series.
the-dramatic-values-in-plautus:
Wilton Wallace Blancké's The Dramatic Values in Plautus was a doctoral thesis at the University of Pennsylvania, dated 1918. Part one sums up past views of Plautus and the proof that his plays were acted. Blancké notes that early praise ran too high, then curbed itself, with bursts of scorn, to a saner mean.

He quotes Cicero, Quintilian, Gellius, and Horace on the Roman comic poet's wit and fine Latin. The study then weighs how the plays work on stage: plot, stock figures, and jokes. It serves students of Latin drama well.
the-gathering-of-brother-hilarius:
Michael Fairless wrote The Gathering of Brother Hilarius as a tale of a monk in the days of the Black Death, first printed in 1901. This copy is the popular edition of 1912.

The preface says a road runs through the book: the white highway Hilarius watched from the monastery gate. The tale may be read, it says, as a romance of plague and a monk with an artist's eyes. Deeper down, it is a tale of the image of God found in plain folk. A dying small maid teaches Hilarius, in silence, the secret of sorrow, sin, death, and love. Fairless wrote The Roadmender in the same grave, spare style.
the-heart-cry-of-jesus:
Byron J. Rees wrote The Heart-Cry of Jesus, and the title page names his earlier works Christlikeness and Hulda, the Pentecostal Prophetess. The book is dedicated to his master, Christ. The introduction, headed The Need of the Day, argues that the modern Holiness movement has created a growing demand for full-salvation books and papers.

Rees, through the introduction, contrasts dry pulpits stocked with science and philosophy against hungry congregations that want bread and meat for the soul. The purpose stated for the book is simple and direct. Little attempt is made at doctrine or dispute. Hungry readers are meant to be led into what the text calls the Canaan life, with rich provision for those already there.
the-history-of-england-volume-i-from-the:
David Hume, Esq., wrote The History of England, Volume I, from the invasion of Julius Caesar to the Revolution in 1688, complete in six volumes with the author's last corrections. A note for this edition explains how footnotes and marginal notes from the printed book are marked in plain text, since Hume's long paragraphs can push a note far from its place.

Before the history stands My Own Life, Hume's short account of himself. It opens by granting that a man can hardly speak long of himself without vanity, so the account will be brief. Readers meet the historian first as his own subject, in a life kept short on purpose.
the-hymns-of-prudentius:
R. Martin Pope translated the hymns of Prudentius into English verse. J. M. Dent and Company published the volume in London in 1905. Its core is the Cathemerinon. Those are hymns for the Christian's day. The opening pages reproduce the poet's Latin preface. The aging writer counts his decades there. White hair proves how many winters have passed. He asks what useful thing his life has done.

His catalogue of his past is candid. A boyhood under the rod comes first. A youth stained by vice follows. Years of legal quarrels came next. Twice he governed noble cities under the laws. A late rise brought him near the emperor. Pope's translation lets English readers meet this poet of Roman Spain. The daily hymns made his name. His self-accusing preface frames them.
the-life-and-adventures-of-santa-claus:
L. Frank Baum gives Santa Claus a full life story, divided into youth, manhood, and old age. Contents trace Claus from a forest foundling in Burzee through his first toy, his first reindeer journey, and the first stockings and Christmas tree. The opening chapter describes that great forest of close trunks and tangled roots.

Baum explains how an immortal child raised by woodland beings learned human sorrow and chose to serve children. Ryls color his toys, Awgwas threaten his work, and the Laughing Valley becomes his home. A kindly origin myth grows from the contents into story.
the-life-of-columbus: A life of Christopher Columbus stands behind this record, yet its opening pages here hold only a glossary and transcriber notes. Only those pages are present, defining terms such as Adelantado for a governor, Arroba for a Spanish weight, Cacique for a West Indies chief, and Cipango for Japan. Notes explain that page headers were moved and long paragraphs split for this edition. No author is named on these pages, and the narrative of Columbus voyages cannot be seen in this record.
the-life-of-jesus: Ernest Renan wrote his life of Jesus from study and travel in the Holy Land, and the Modern Library issued this edition in New York. Only the title pages and Renan dedication to his sister Henriette are present here, noting her death at Byblus on September 24, 1861. His note recalls long days at Ghazir where she sat beside him while he wrote, visiting the places with him. An introduction by John Haynes Holmes is noted as missing from this text. The life itself cannot be seen in this record.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-0:
Volume two of Suetonius's Lives of the Twelve Caesars is given to Augustus, in Alexander Thomson's translation revised by T. Forester. Suetonius begins, as he often does, with the family. The Octavii were of the first distinction in Velitrae. A street there bore their name. An altar honored an Octavius who snatched a sacrifice half raw from the fire, marched out, and returned victorious. From that legend he traces the family's path through Roman ranks.

Tarquinius Priscus admitted them to the senate, Servius Tullius placed them among the patricians, and after a long spell in the plebeian order Julius Caesar restored their patrician rank. Readers get ancestry and omen first, the habit of a biographer who explains an emperor through his house.

Tiberius receives the third volume of Suetonius's Lives of the Twelve Caesars, in the Thomson translation revised by T. Forester. The life opens with the patrician Claudii, who came from Regilli, a Sabine town, soon after Rome was built. They arrived with a great body of dependants, received lands beyond the Anio from the state, and won a burying-place near the Capitol.

Suetonius totals the family's honors: twenty-eight consulships, five dictatorships, seven censorships, seven triumphs, and two ovations. He also notes a family quirk, the rejection of the praenomen Lucius after one bearer was convicted of robbery and another of murder. The proud, severe Claudian stock sets the stage for Tiberius himself.

Claudius is the subject of volume five in Suetonius's Lives of the Twelve Caesars, in the Thomson translation as revised by T. Forester. The opening belongs to his father Drusus. Drusus was born to Livia three months after her marriage to Augustus. That timing fed suspicion about his parentage, and a popular verse joked about great children arriving in three months. Drusus campaigned in Raetia and Germany. He was the first Roman general to navigate the Northern Ocean.

Suetonius adds a marvel: a barbarian woman of superhuman size appeared to Drusus and forbade him, in Latin, to advance farther. Drusus dug great trenches beyond the Rhine that still bore his name. Readers meet Claudius through a famous father's glory before the emperor himself appears.

Aulus Vitellius fills volume nine of Suetonius's Lives of the Twelve Caesars, translated by Alexander Thomson and revised by T. Forester. Suetonius admits at once that accounts of the family disagree: some call the Vitellii ancient and noble, others recent, obscure, and even mean. He suspects flatterers and detractors of the emperor shaped both versions, unless the family's fortunes simply varied over time.

He then reports a memoir claiming that the Vitellii descended from Faunus, king of the aborigines, and from Vitellia, worshipped in many places as a goddess. They supposedly reigned over all Latium, then moved from Sabine country to Rome and joined the patricians. Readers see a biographer weighing rival traditions instead of settling them by fiat.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-1:
Titus Flavius Vespasianus Augustus, Vespasian's son, is the subject of volume eleven in Suetonius's Lives, translated by Alexander Thomson and revised by T. Forester. Suetonius calls Titus the darling and delight of mankind, a striking verdict because Titus had lived under public dislike before becoming emperor. He was born on December 30, in the year famous for the death of Caius, in a mean house and a small, dark room near the Septizonium.

Titus was educated in the palace alongside Britannicus, Claudius's son, under the same masters. A face-reader brought to examine Britannicus declared that Britannicus would never be emperor, but Titus, standing by, would. Titus was even thought to have tasted the poison that killed Britannicus at table. Favor and danger run together from the start of this life.
the-lost-stradivarius: Only the Penguin Books author-biography pages for J. Meade Falkner's The Lost Stradivarius (1895) are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. The biography describes Falkner, born in 1858 and educated at Marlborough and Hertford College, Oxford, as both scholar and captain of industry. He rose at the Armstrong-Whitworth firm to chairman from 1915 to 1920, studied manuscripts in the Vatican Library, collected missals, and died at Durham in 1932. His other novels named are The Nebuly Coat and Moonfleet.
the-old-english-physiologus:
Albert Stanbrough Cook edited The Old English Physiologus for Yale Studies in English, published in 1921. Cook, a Yale professor of English, supplied the text and a prose translation. James Hall Pitman, a fellow in English at Yale, supplied a verse translation. A facsimile of the old manuscript page faces the text.

The Physiologus is a medieval bestiary in Old English verse, giving the lore of beasts with moral lessons. The first piece treats the panther, one of countless kinds of birds and beasts on earth. The three versions run in short alternating sections so readers can compare the Old English with both modern renderings line by line.
the-pony-rider-boys-in-montana-or-the-my:
Frank Gee Patchin's The Pony Rider Boys in Montana opens at the start of a journey, Chapter I being titled Fitting Out for the Journey. A Northern Pacific train slows at Forsythe, and four boys get down: Tad Butler, Walter Perkins, Ned Rector, and Stacy Brown, called Chunky. Their companion is Professor Zepplin. He is a tall, athletic man whose iron gray beard and deeply bronzed face make him look fiercer than he is.

The boys wear the regulation suits of the cowboy, faded from long service on the open plains. They pull their belongings from the racks with practised ease. On the platform a man in a business suit and a broad brimmed sombrero steps up without hesitation. Smiling, he asks whether they are the Pony Rider Boys. Patchin's series follows the same four boys and their professor through a fresh western country in each volume.
the-reign-of-tiberius-out-of-the-first-s:
Thomas Gordon's translation of Tacitus, edited by Arthur Galton, gathers the first six books of the Annals together with the treatise on Germany and the life of Agricola. Galton opens his introduction by borrowing Gordon's own praise of Tacitus for wisdom and force.

The contents promise a reign study built book by book, plus accounts of German customs and of Agricola's Britain with its climate and peoples. A Horace motto crowns the title page. Readers who want Rome under Tiberius in a classic English version will find Gordon's devotion to his author part of the appeal.
the-revolt-on-venus:
Carey Rockwell's Tom Corbett adventure was copyrighted in 1954. Rockhill Radio held that copyright. Grosset and Dunlap issued the book at New York. Louis Glanzman supplied the illustrations. Willy Ley served as technical adviser for the science. Series pages list companion cadet stories for boys. Those books treat Mars, deep space, and pirates at large. Pioneers in space complete the advertised list for young readers.

Only the title pages are present here in this record. The series list and the copyright notice appear with them. No chapter text follows those opening pages at all. The Venus adventure itself does not appear on these pages. Readers meet the packaging of a boys' space series here. Its promise is cadet training, rockets, and revolt on another world.
the-roman-pronunciation-of-latin-why-we-: Frances E. Lord, professor of Latin at Wellesley College, published her guide with Ginn and Company at Boston in 1894. An encoding note in these pages explains marks for long and short vowels, transliterated Greek, boldface, and italics for electronic readers. Here only that note and the title page are present, so Lord's pronunciation guidance itself does not appear.
the-teaching-of-jesus: The Rev. George Jackson's Teaching of Jesus, dated 1903 and dedicated to his four children, is shown here through its title page and contents only. The contents arrange his subject under plain heads: an introduction, then chapters concerning God, concerning Jesus himself, concerning his death, and further topics beyond the cut. Each chapter carries Gospel texts, such as 'Holy Father' and 'Who say ye that I am?' Jackson's own teaching voice does not appear in the pages present, though his orderly, Scripture-first plan is easy to see.
the-world-english-bible-web-exodus:
Exodus, book two of the World English Bible, lists Jacob's sons who entered Egypt. Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah lead the names. Seventy souls in all came from Jacob's line. Joseph and his brothers eventually die in Egypt. Their descendants multiply until the land fills with them. Then a new king arises who never knew Joseph.

That king fears Israel's growing strength. He worries they might join Egypt's enemies in war. Oppression follows, and with it Moses' birth. Deliverance through plagues and sea crossing dominates the book. Lawgiving at Sinai completes Israel's founding story. Exodus remains central to Jewish and Christian memory alike.
the-world-english-bible-web-leviticus:
Book three in the World English Bible, Leviticus, starts at the Tent of Meeting. God calls Moses and gives rules for offerings. Israelites may bring animals from herd or flock. A burnt offering must be a male without blemish. The worshiper lays a hand on its head. Atonement is made through that act, the text says.

Aaron's sons then present and sprinkle the blood. The animal is skinned and cut into pieces. Detailed ritual instruction fills the whole book. Holiness codes govern food, purity, and festivals. Priests mediate between a holy God and the camp. Readers gain the rulebook behind ancient Israel's worship life.
the-wreck-of-the-hesperus:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's ballad The Wreck of the Hesperus appears in an illustrated 1889 New York edition. An introduction explains its setting at Norman's Woe. That rocky headland lies between Gloucester and Magnolia in Massachusetts. A real disaster there had faded from memory. Longfellow chose the spot as background for his poem. The introduction admits the schooner actually struck nearer Gloucester.

The critic praises the ballad's quaint, old-time style. Its rhythm carries trampling waves and crashing timbers. Careless readers, the introduction warns, miss much of its art. Thoughtful readers find force hidden under its simplicity. The poem made Norman's Woe famous in American memory.
theaetetus:
Benjamin Jowett translated Plato's Theaetetus, and his introduction analyzes the dialogue's character. Some Platonic dialogues, Jowett notes, resist being dated by style. The Theaetetus resembles both early and later writings. Its style, humor, and dramatic interest suggest Plato's best period. Its fruitless search for knowledge suggests the early dialogues. Socrates there still professes ignorance and plays the midwife.

Jowett weighs these competing signs carefully. He leans toward grouping it with the Apology and Phaedrus. Yet its subject matter links it to later works. The dialogue asks what knowledge itself is. Readers get both a classic translation and a scholar's map of its puzzles. Jowett's Victorian Plato shaped English philosophy teaching for decades.
thoughts-of-marcus-aurelius:
Edwin Ginn edited George Long's translation of the Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus for use as a school reader. Contents promise a preface, a biographical sketch, the thoughts themselves, an essay on Marcus's philosophy, and an index. The preface defends giving children serious books.

Ginn argues the young like being treated as capable of appreciating good things. Marcus, who took the philosopher's robe at twelve, practised his own precepts rather than only prescribing for others. Readers get a Roman emperor's private reflections, presented as generous, sweet, and humble guidance for every age.
timaeus:
Plato's Timaeus, translated by Benjamin Jowett, opens with an introduction and analysis in eight sections. Jowett calls the dialogue Plato's most obscure work for modern readers, yet the most influential over the ancient and medieval worlds. Its obscurity grows from early physical science.

Theology, mathematics, and physiology are confused together, Jowett argues, while thinkers sought nature's whole without knowing its parts. Ancient philosophers looked from earth to stars for guidance and hung between matter and mind. Readers get Plato's cosmology of creation and nature, framed by a candid warning about its difficulty and historical power.
titus-andronicus: Editorial notes by Michael S. Hart open this record, explaining old printers' spelling in Shakespeare texts, as in the sibling Timon record. Type packed into cliches ran short, so u and v swap and double v replaces w. Oddly, the note closes by naming a different play, Shakespeare's First Part of Henry the Sixth, although this record is titled for Titus Andronicus. No scene from either play follows. Readers get the editor's spelling defence and that title clash, while the tragedy itself does not appear here.
tobogganing-on-parnassus: Franklin P. Adams dedicated his verse collection to Bert Leston Taylor, called his guide and philosopher but, pointedly, not his friend in the dedication's joke. A prefatory poem hopes one glad heart or single smile would satisfy him as a singer, quoting Locker's phrasing. Contents list light poems titled Us Poets, Rubber-Stamp Humour, Carpe Diem or Cop the Day, and Horace the Wise. The dedication verse and contents are what is present here, so Adams's poems themselves do not appear.
toby-tyler-or-ten-weeks-with-a-circus:
James Otis opens his boys' story at a circus candy booth, where a very small boy asks whether six peanuts for a cent is really the limit. Toby Tyler holds his purchase wistfully, cracks the largest nut, and finds it bad. The vendor surprises him by tossing two more nuts.

Asked his name, Toby admits it may not truly belong to him; the fellows and Uncle Dan'l call him so. Uncle Dan'l is no uncle at all, just the man he lives with. Readers get a child's circus adventure beginning with peanuts, kindness from a stern vendor, and an orphan's uncertain name.
trial-of-the-witnesses-of-the-resurrecti:
First published about 1729, The Trial of the Witnesses of the Resurrection of Jesus stages a legal debate among gentlemen of the inns of court. The talk turns on Woolston, lately tried and convicted for discourses against Christ's miracles. One man admires Woolston's arguments and thinks them unanswerable.

A lawyer in the company answers that evidence has weight and rules. No one, he says, would settle a five-shilling property claim on proof that thin. The company then resolves to argue the resurrection like counsel, witness by witness. Readers who enjoy theology argued as courtroom procedure will find the whole method set out in the opening pages.
un-un-res-first-report-on-the-united-nat:
Cyprus got a United Nations peacekeeping force in 1964, and this first report on the force records its early days. Fighting between Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot groups had pushed the island toward war. The Security Council sent the force, UNFICYP, to keep the peace and restore calm.

The report describes the force's arrival, its patrols, and its talks with both sides. It covers early clashes, blocked roads, and efforts to return life to normal. Nobody then guessed the force would still be on the island decades later. The report is the opening page of that long story.
un-un-res-second-report-on-the-united-na:
A second report on the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus follows the force through its first months in 1964. UNFICYP had arrived that spring to stop fighting between the island's Greek and Turkish communities. The calm it guarded was thin, and armed posts still faced each other in many towns.

The report describes patrol work, local truces, and efforts to reopen roads and markets. It also covers the force's talks with both leaderships about limits on armed men. The text shows a young mission learning its trade, and an island settling into a division that would last.
weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-speech-:
Titus is book 56 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. Paul writes to Titus, his true child in their shared faith. Paul left him in Crete to set right what still lacked order. Elders were to be named in every town.

An elder, Paul says, must live a clean life and stay true to one wife. He must not be quick to anger, a hard drinker, or greedy for gain. Guests should find his home open, and his mind should stay sober and self-ruled. Weymouth sets out the rules in crisp, plain lists. Readers get a brief guide to sound church order.
what-dress-makes-of-us:
Dorothy Quigley wrote What Dress Makes of Us, printed in 1897 with drawings by Annie Blakeslee. Parts first ran in the New York Sun and the New York Journal. Her preface laughs at the odd power of clothes to make people look absurd. A short round coat, she says, can make a stout man look like a jug.

A tilted bonnet can give a sober matron a tipsy air. One famed Oxford divine was even taken for a spinster due to his odd hat and coat. Quigley uses such tales to show how dress shapes first views. The book mixes humor with sharp notes on taste.
woman-s-trials-or-tales-and-sketches-fro:
T. S. Arthur published these tales in Philadelphia in 1851. His preface states the aim plainly. The stories seek sympathy for women in the hard trials of daily life. Arthur says people think too much about their own troubles. Fiction can turn their thoughts toward others who suffer. Right feeling, he argues, leads to right action.

The contents promise stories about patience, taking in boarders, and plain sewing as charity. One tale follows a woman named Jessie Hampton. Arthur planned the volume as the first of twelve household books. Each story works as a small moral lesson drawn from ordinary life.
